title: Popconfirm
wrapsNative: confirmationDialog(_:isPresented:titleVisibility:actions:message:) on the button, shown as a popover anchored to it at regular width; popover(isPresented:arrowEdge:content:) with presentationCompactAdaptation(.popover) when it must stay anchored on a phone
summary: A small confirmation tied to the button that asked is the system confirmation dialog, anchored to the button on an iPad; for a phone, a popover kept as a popover. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: Before a small, local action that is hard to undo, started from a control on screen: removing a filter, revoking one invitation, clearing a field.
whenNotToUse: For actions that are easy to undo, act at once and offer Undo (see undo-toast). For deleting something important, or with consequences to list, use an alert or a sheet (see confirm-dialog).
api: func confirmationDialog(_ title: String, isPresented: Binding<Bool>, titleVisibility: Visibility = .automatic, actions: () -> some View, message: () -> some View) -> some View
func popover(isPresented: Binding<Bool>, arrowEdge: Edge = .top, content: () -> some View) -> some View
func presentationCompactAdaptation(_ adaptation: PresentationAdaptation) -> some View

states.name: compact width
states.description: The confirmation dialog rises from the bottom of an iPhone with the destructive button and Cancel.

states.name: regular width
states.description: On an iPad the same dialog is a popover with an arrow pointing at the button.

states.name: anchored popover
states.description: With the popover recipe the question and its two buttons stay next to the button at every width.

appearance: The confirmation dialog is drawn by the system in every theme, with the destructive button in the system's red. The popover recipe uses the theme's raised background, Monarch text styles and a danger MonarchButton.
platformNotes: The web Popconfirm is a popover with a title, a description, confirm and cancel buttons, a danger tone, a pending state while onConfirm runs, and an error line. On iOS the confirmation dialog anchors to its button on an iPad but is a bottom sheet on an iPhone; the popover recipe keeps it anchored everywhere. The system dialog closes when a button is tapped, so run the action afterwards and show its progress and failure on the screen; the popover recipe can keep a loading button instead. initialFocus has no equivalent: VoiceOver starts at the top. Android composes a small dialog.
accessibility: System behaviour: the dialog is modal; VoiceOver reads the title and message, and the escape gesture chooses Cancel.
Name the destructive button after the action ("Remove"), so it does not depend on its colour.
In the popover recipe, mark the question with the header trait and give the buttons the 44-point targets of MonarchButton.
edgeCases: titleVisibility: .visible is needed for the question to show on an iPhone.
Only one dialog or popover is shown at a time.
In a List row, attach the dialog to the button, not the row, so the iPad popover points at the button.

examples.title: Remove a filter
Anchored to the button on a phone too

title: Popover
wrapsNative: popover(isPresented:attachmentAnchor:arrowEdge:content:) with presentationCompactAdaptation(.popover)
summary: A floating panel anchored to a control is the SwiftUI popover. With presentationCompactAdaptation(.popover) it stays a popover on a phone instead of becoming a sheet. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: For a small amount of interactive content that belongs to one control: a filter panel, a quick edit, a short explanation with a link.
whenNotToUse: Not for a list of actions (use Menu), not for text that only names a control (use help and an accessibility hint), and not for a task with several steps or a keyboard-heavy form on a phone (use sheet).
api: func popover<Content: View>(isPresented: Binding<Bool>, attachmentAnchor: PopoverAttachmentAnchor = .rect(.bounds), arrowEdge: Edge? = nil, content: @escaping () -> Content) -> some View
func presentationCompactAdaptation(_ adaptation: PresentationAdaptation) -> some View
func presentationBackground<S: ShapeStyle>(_ style: S) -> some View

states.name: open
states.description: The system draws the panel with an arrow pointing at the anchor. A tap outside closes it.

states.name: adapted
states.description: Without presentationCompactAdaptation the popover becomes a sheet at compact width.

appearance: The system draws the panel, its arrow and its shadow in every theme. presentationBackground with the theme's raised background colour makes the panel match Monarch surfaces; the content uses Monarch components.
platformNotes: The web Popover is non-modal: the page behind stays interactive. An iOS popover takes the first tap outside to dismiss itself, so the content behind it cannot be used while it is open. The web's side and align are arrowEdge and attachmentAnchor; the system moves the panel when there is no room. The web's PopoverClose is a button that sets isPresented to false. Android builds a MonarchPopover because Compose has no anchored panel with an arrow; iOS has one, so nothing is built here.
accessibility: System behaviour: VoiceOver focus moves into the popover when it opens and is confined to it; the escape gesture closes it and focus returns to the anchor.
The popover has no title of its own; start the content with a heading, marked with accessibilityAddTraits(.isHeader).
Give the popover a way to close that is not a tap outside when it contains a form: a Done button.
edgeCases: The popover sizes itself to its content. Give long text a width with frame(idealWidth:) so it wraps instead of growing across the screen.
At the largest text sizes the content may be taller than the screen; put it in a ScrollView.
Without presentationCompactAdaptation the same code shows a sheet on a phone, so test both widths.

examples.title: Filters
examples.template:
MonarchButton({{trigger}}) { isShown = true }
    .popover(isPresented: $isShown, arrowEdge: .top) {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: theme.spacing.space3) {
            Toggle({{options.0.label}}, isOn: $first)
                .toggleStyle(.monarchCheckbox)
                .monarchTextStyle(.body)
            Toggle({{options.1.label}}, isOn: $second)
                .toggleStyle(.monarchCheckbox)
                .monarchTextStyle(.body)
        }
        .foregroundStyle(theme.colors.textDefault)
        .padding(theme.spacing.space4)
        .accessibilityElement(children: .contain)
        .accessibilityLabel({{label}})
        .presentationCompactAdaptation(.popover)
        .presentationBackground(theme.colors.bgRaised)
    }

    .popover(isPresented: $isShown, arrowEdge: .top) {

                .toggleStyle(.monarchCheckbox)
                .monarchTextStyle(.body)
            Toggle("Unassigned", isOn: $second)
                .toggleStyle(.monarchCheckbox)
                .monarchTextStyle(.body)
        }
        .foregroundStyle(theme.colors.textDefault)
        .padding(theme.spacing.space4)
        .accessibilityElement(children: .contain)
        .accessibilityLabel("Filters")
        .presentationCompactAdaptation(.popover)
        .presentationBackground(theme.colors.bgRaised)
    }

summary: A post in a community feed or search result: author, relative time, pinned and answered markers, tags, title, a short excerpt, and reaction and comment counts.

states.description: The preview slot fills the 4:3 area.

states.name: camera off or audio call
states.description: A muted placeholder with a crossed-out camera and "Camera is off".

states.name: camera starting
states.description: The placeholder reads "Starting camera…".

states.name: problem

appearance: The preview area uses the muted background colour with muted text and a rounded container shape. The toggles keep MonarchCallControls' look (danger when a device is off). The meter uses MonarchAudioLevelMeter's colours. Join is a primary button and Cancel a ghost button. All follow the theme in light, dark and both high-contrast themes.
platformNotes: The web lobby takes a MediaStream and measures the microphone with Web Audio itself; on iOS Monarch captures nothing: the app fills the preview slot (AVCaptureVideoPreviewLayer in a UIViewRepresentable) and passes the level it measures (AVAudioRecorder or AVAudioEngine metering). The web toggles are labelled "Join muted" and "Join with camera off"; iOS uses MonarchCallControls' standard toggles, read as Microphone or Camera, on or off. The web mirrors the video; mirroring is the app's preview layer's job on iOS. The web takes device picker props; iOS takes a devices slot. The web's onJoin receives the settings; on iOS the app already owns them through the bindings. Android has no lobby yet. Status experimental: it is a product composite until a Rook app adopts it.
accessibility: The heading has the header trait.
The preview is a container named Your camera preview; its placeholder icon and text are one element.
The microphone and camera are standard toggles in a group named Microphone and camera, read with their on or off state; the symbol changes as well as the colour.
The level meter is MonarchAudioLevelMeter named Microphone level.
The avatars and "2 already in the call" are read as one element.
An error is shown with an icon and text, not colour alone.
Join and Cancel are standard buttons of at least 44 points; Join reads Joining… while busy.
edgeCases: An audio level outside 0 to 1, or not a number, is clamped to the range.
isCameraOn left out means an audio call: no camera toggle and the Camera is off placeholder.
An error wins over the camera state, so the preview slot is not shown while there is a problem.
Long titles and join titles wrap; the action row stacks at large text sizes.

platformNotes: The web opens a popover from the "+N" button and makes each avatar a button. On iOS overlapping 24-point avatars cannot each be a 44-point touch target, so the whole stack is one button that opens a sheet, and people are tapped in that list. On iPad and Mac the sheet appears as a form sheet. Voice Control accepts the initials shown on an avatar through accessibilityInputLabels, where the web adds them to the button's name.
accessibility: The stack is named "5 people here".
A stack that opens the list is one button whose value names each visible person with their presence and activity, then "2 more", with the hint "Shows everyone here".
A stack that does not open the list is a container whose avatars are images named "Ana Silva, Online, Editing".
Presence is always spoken, with the custom status, so it never depends on the dot colour.
Each row in the list is one element with the same text, at least 44 points high, and a button when onPersonTap is given.
Voice Control accepts a person's name or the initials shown on their avatar.
Avatars, dots and text scale with Dynamic Type.
edgeCases: An empty list of people draws nothing.
With one person more than maxVisible, every avatar is shown instead of a "+1" tile.
An activity that is empty or white space is left out.
Long names and activities wrap in the list.

The web positions an overlay dot itself; on iOS place it with overlay(alignment: .bottomTrailing). The web's hover title has no counterpart on touch. The custom status is one string here, where the web takes an emoji and a text.
accessibility: The dot is one element read as its text, such as "Away · In a meeting".
Do not disturb has a bar and offline is a ring in every setting; with Differentiate Without Colour, away is half-filled and busy is a square, so all five differ by form.
isDecorative hides the dot when the presence is already in text beside it.
The dot scales with Dynamic Type.
The dot is not interactive and has no touch target.
edgeCases: A custom status of only white space is ignored.
Without Differentiate Without Colour, online, away and busy differ by colour only for sighted users; show the presence in text where it matters.
The half-filled away dot fills its leading half, so it mirrors in right-to-left layouts.

whenToUse: In an import flow, after the columns are mapped and before the import runs, so people can see which rows will be imported, which have warnings and which will be skipped.
whenNotToUse: Not for browsing data that is already stored (use a List or Table) and not for comparing two records (use MonarchDuplicatePanel or MonarchMergeDialog).

options.name: caption
options.description: The spoken name of the rows, for example "Preview of contacts.csv".

options.name: rows
options.description: The rows of the file in file order: number, values by column id, optional status override, errors, warnings and a note.

options.name: columns
options.description: The data columns shown in each row, in order. isNumeric draws tabular digits.

options.name: filter
options.description: The chosen filter when the app owns it; nil keeps it inside the view, starting at all.

options.name: isFilterable
options.description: Whether filter tabs with counts are shown when some rows are not ready.

options.name: pageSize
options.description: Rows shown before the load more control; each load shows one more page. 0 shows every row.

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for every built-in string: tab names, status names, the row title, the spoken empty value and the empty states.

states.name: mixed results
states.description: Filter tabs appear: All, then Error, Warning, Duplicate and Ready, each with its count, only for results that have rows.

states.name: all ready
states.description: No filter tabs; the rows are shown with a Ready badge.

states.name: filtered
states.description: Only rows with the chosen result. Changing the filter goes back to the first page.

states.name: filter matches nothing
states.description: MonarchEmptyState of the filtered kind with a clear filters button that goes back to All.

states.name: empty file
states.description: MonarchEmptyState "No rows to preview" with the message that the file has no data rows.

states.name: paged
states.description: After pageSize rows, MonarchLoadMore shows how many of the filtered rows are shown and loads the next page.

appearance: Each row is a card on the surface fill with a subtle border. The result badge uses the success, warning, danger or info tone with its own symbol. Value labels and the dash for an empty value use the muted text colour; error issues use the strong danger colour and warnings the strong warning colour, each with an icon.
platformNotes: The web shows a table with Row, Result, the data columns and Issues on wide screens and cards on narrow ones, with a page navigator. On iOS each row is a card at every width, the native form of a row on a phone; the plan named List rows, but a List cannot sit inside the scroll view of an import screen, so the rows are a lazy stack the app puts in its ScrollView. Paging is a load more control instead of page numbers. Cell values and the note are plain strings, where the web accepts any content. Android uses the same name and options.
accessibility: The rows are a container named by caption.
Each row is one element: the label is its title ("Row 4") and the value reads the result, every column with its value, each issue after its kind ("Error: Email: Not a valid address") and the note.
A missing value is drawn as a dash and read as "Empty".
The result is shown by a badge with a symbol and a name, and each issue by an icon of its kind, as well as by colour.
The filter tabs are MonarchTabs: a tab bar named "Show rows" whose tabs read their name and count.
Text scales with Dynamic Type; values and issues wrap.
edgeCases: A status given on the row wins over its errors and warnings, so a duplicate with warnings is counted as a duplicate.
A row with errors and warnings is an error row; both lists are shown.
A chosen filter whose result has no rows keeps its tab, with a count of 0.
Several rows with the same row number are not supported: the row number is the identity.

appearance: Checks use the strong success colour and dashes the subtle text colour; not-included feature names on a page use the muted text colour. Plan names are subheading text, prices title text, suffixes, notes and descriptions caption text in the muted colour. A highlighted grid header has an accent border; rows are separated by MonarchDivider. Colours come from theme roles in every theme.
platformNotes: The web PricingTable is one real table that scrolls sideways on narrow screens with the feature column pinned, and also exports BillingPeriodToggle and helper functions. On iOS a phone shows one plan per page instead (the plan comparison stays readable at large text sizes), the grid is used at regular width, and the period picker is a standard segmented Picker; the picker's suffix is shown as a caption under it rather than inside the segment. hideCaption has no meaning: the caption is the spoken name of the container. Android ships the same MonarchPricingTable.
accessibility: The table is a container labelled "Plan comparison" (or labels.caption).
Plan names and group titles have the header trait.
In the grid each cell is one element read as the plan, the feature and "Included", "Not included" or the text, such as "Team, Single sign-on: Included".
On a page each feature is one element read as its name, its value and its description.
Checks and dashes are hidden from VoiceOver; the words carry the value, so nothing depends on colour or shape alone.
The billing period and plan pickers are standard segmented Pickers with their own names.
The price and its suffix are read together.
edgeCases: More than five plans make grid columns narrow; use pages or fewer plans.
Long feature names and values wrap; grid columns share the width.
At accessibility text sizes automatic uses pages even on a wide screen.
The pages scroll sideways with paging; the plan picker follows the visible page. Swiping between pages with VoiceOver was not tried on a device.
Segmented pickers shorten long period or plan names; keep them short.

title: PriorityPicker
wrapsNative: A Button trigger and a popover of Buttons in a VStack, with the level's own tone on each icon (a system Menu draws every icon in the tint); Picker with .pickerStyle(.menu) and a Label per level remains the choice for the system menu
summary: Shows and changes how urgent an issue is, on the urgent, high, medium, low and no-priority scale, with the standard menu picker. Monarch ships no type.
whenToUse: In issue rows, cards and detail screens where the priority can be changed. Give every level its own SF Symbol and name, as in the examples.
whenNotToUse: For a read-only priority, show the Label without a menu. For the severity of incidents or alerts, use MonarchStatusBadge or a tone.
api: Picker(_ title: String, selection: Binding<SelectionValue>, content: () -> Content)
func pickerStyle(_ style: MenuPickerStyle) -> some View
Label(_ title: String, systemImage: String)
Menu(content: () -> Content, label: () -> Label)

states.name: selected
states.description: The menu shows a checkmark next to the current level; the trigger shows its name (and, in the Menu form, its symbol).

states.name: disabled
states.description: System dimming, with disabled(_:).

appearance: System menu in every theme. In the Menu form the trigger takes the Monarch button style and the symbol takes a theme role: the strong danger colour for urgent, the strong warning colour for high, the default text colour for medium and low, and the muted text colour for no priority. Inside the system menu the symbols take the menu's own colour, so the shape and the name carry the level.
platformNotes: The web ships PriorityPicker with drawn glyphs (an exclamation tile, three, two or one bars, dashes) and Android builds MonarchPriorityPicker. On iOS the standard menu picker already gives the menu, the checkmark, keyboard and VoiceOver behaviour, so Monarch ships no type. A system menu shows SF Symbols, not custom drawings, so the levels use distinct symbols: exclamationmark.square.fill, chevron.up, equal, chevron.down and minus (chevron.up.2 needs iOS 18). The web's priorityFromNumber and priorityToNumber (0 none, 1 urgent, 2 high, 3 medium, 4 low) belong in the app's model. The web's level none is called unset in the examples, because none reads as Optional.none in Swift.
accessibility: System behaviour: the picker is read as a pop-up button with the current level as its value; the menu items are read by name with the selected one marked.
In the Menu form, accessibilityLabel("Priority: High") names the trigger with the current level, as the web does.
Every level has its own symbol and its own name, so the level never depends on colour.
A symbol-only trigger needs monarchMinimumHitTarget() for a 44-point touch target.
edgeCases: Offer a subset of levels by listing fewer cases in the ForEach.
A long translated level name wraps in the trigger at large text sizes; the menu truncates as the system does.

title: PrivacyChoicesLink
wrapsNative: Button with Label and the Monarch link style, opening sheet(isPresented:content:) with a NavigationStack, a Form with one Toggle (switch), a Link and ToolbarItem Cancel and Save
summary: A recipe, not a component: a "Your privacy choices" row in settings that opens a sheet with one switch to allow or stop the sale or sharing of personal information.
whenToUse: In settings, for people in regions where they may opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information (opt-out regimes such as the California rules).
whenNotToUse: Where consent is asked before any optional use (opt-in regimes), ask with the full consent preferences instead. For tracking across other companies' apps and websites, iOS requires the AppTrackingTransparency prompt; this switch does not replace it.
api: Button { … } label: { Label("Your privacy choices", systemImage: "hand.raised") }.buttonStyle(.monarchLink(.standalone))
.sheet(isPresented: $isOpen) { NavigationStack { Form { Toggle("Allow sale or sharing", isOn: $draft) } } }
ToolbarItem(placement: .cancellationAction) { Button("Cancel") { … } }
ToolbarItem(placement: .confirmationAction) { Button("Save") { … } }

states.name: hidden
states.description: Outside opt-out regions the row is not shown.

states.name: open
states.description: A sheet with what sale or sharing means, the switch with its help line, the policy link, and Cancel and Save in the toolbar. The switch starts from the stored choice.

states.name: locked by signal
states.description: When the account carries a Global Privacy Control opt-out, the switch is off and disabled and the help line says why.

states.name: saved
states.description: Save stores the switch; Cancel leaves the stored choice unchanged.

appearance: The row is a standalone Monarch link with an icon. The sheet is a system Form with the standard switch, the body text style for the explanation and an external Monarch link to the policy, all in the theme colours.
platformNotes: The web's PrivacyChoicesLink is a footer link component with a dialog and its own strings. On iOS it is a recipe: a settings row opening a sheet with a Form, the native place for a setting. A native app receives no browser Global Privacy Control header, so the lock applies only when the app knows of a signal for the account (for example from its website); otherwise leave it out. The web's showIn regimes are the app's own region check. The web shows a policy link from policyHref or policyLink; here it is a Link. The official California privacy choices icon is the app's to add as an image; the recipe uses an SF Symbol. Android composes the same recipe.
accessibility: The row is a button whose label is the text; the icon is part of the Label.
The switch is a standard Toggle, read as "Allow sale or sharing" with its on or off value.
When the switch is locked, the reason is the visible section footer, which VoiceOver reads with the form.
Cancel and Save are standard toolbar buttons in the cancellation and confirmation placements.
The policy link is a standard Link marked as external.
edgeCases: Show the row only where the opt-out applies, decided by the app's region logic.
Opening the sheet starts from the stored choice, so a cancelled change does not linger.
A signal lock keeps sale and sharing off whatever was stored before.

name: MonarchCircularProgressViewStyle
title: ProgressCircle
wrapsNative: ProgressView, ProgressViewStyle
summary: A progress ring in Monarch's colours for the standard ProgressView, determinate or indeterminate, with the value in the middle of the large ring.
whenToUse: For progress with a known fraction in a small space: an upload in a row, a quota, a step count on a card.
whenNotToUse: For a short wait of unknown length, use the standard circular ProgressView (the spinner). For progress across the width of a region, use the linear style, monarchLinear.
api: static var monarchCircular: MonarchCircularProgressViewStyle
static func monarchCircular(tone: MonarchTone? = nil, size: MonarchCircularProgressSize = .md, showsValue: Bool = false) -> MonarchCircularProgressViewStyle
init(tone: MonarchTone? = nil, size: MonarchCircularProgressSize = .md, showsValue: Bool = false)
enum MonarchCircularProgressSize { case sm, md, lg }

options.name: tone
options.description: The colour of the arc. nil is the accent tone, the same as .accent.

options.name: size
options.description: The diameter: sm 20, md 32, lg 48, xl 72 points, scaled with Dynamic Type.

options.name: showsValue
options.description: Draws the value in the middle of the ring. Only the lg size has room for it.

states.name: determinate
states.description: The arc starts at the top and covers the completed fraction, limited to 0 through 1.

states.name: complete
states.description: A full ring.

states.name: indeterminate
states.description: A quarter arc turns; it stays still when Reduce Motion is on.

appearance: A muted track with a round-capped arc in the accent colour, or in the solid colour of the tone, in every theme. The value and the label use the default text colour.
platformNotes: The parity map expected this as the circular form of MonarchProgressViewStyle. That type is the linear style and takes no parameters, so the ring is its own style type, MonarchCircularProgressViewStyle, reached with .monarchCircular; the two can be merged later without changing call sites. SwiftUI's own circular style ignores the value on iOS, which is why the ring is drawn here. Sizes are sm, md, lg and xl (20, 32, 48 and 72 points) as the web, which also has xs (16). The accent is the absence of a tone, because MonarchTone has no accent case; the info tone is also accepted. The web formatValue function is covered by ProgressView's currentValueLabel. The label of the ProgressView is drawn after the ring, where the web label is only an accessible name. Android themes the Material 3 CircularProgressIndicator.
accessibility: The ring and the label are one element whose value is the whole percentage in the environment's locale.
The element has the updates-frequently trait.
There is no built-in name: give the ProgressView a label, or accessibilityLabel, that says what is in progress.
The value in the middle of the ring is hidden from VoiceOver, because the element already has it as its value.
The indeterminate arc does not turn when Reduce Motion is on.
The tone is colour only. Say what it means in the label.
The ring, its stroke and the text scale with Dynamic Type.
edgeCases: A value above the total draws a full ring; a not-a-number fraction draws an empty one.
showsValue has no effect on the sm and md sizes, or without a value.
A currentValueLabel given to the ProgressView replaces the percentage in the middle of the ring; it shrinks to half its size before it is cut.
The arc always runs clockwise from the top, also in right-to-left layouts.

title: PromptDialog
wrapsNative: alert(_:isPresented:actions:message:) with a TextField in its actions
summary: Asking for one short value is the system alert with a TextField among its actions. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: To ask for a single short value without leaving the screen: a name for a saved view, a new name for a group, a link address.
whenNotToUse: Not when the value must be checked before the dialog closes, is more than one line, or is saved while the dialog shows progress: the alert closes on any button. Use a sheet with MonarchTextField for those, as in the second example.
api: func alert<A: View, M: View>(_ title: String, isPresented: Binding<Bool>, actions: () -> A, message: () -> M) -> some View
TextField(_ title: String, text: Binding<String>)
Button(_ title: String, role: ButtonRole?, action: () -> Void)

states.name: presented
states.description: The system alert with the title, the message, the field and the buttons. The keyboard opens with the field focused.

states.name: dismissed
states.description: Any button closes the alert. The cancel role also answers the escape gesture.

appearance: The alert is drawn by the system in every theme. Monarch colours, type and the Monarch text field are not applied inside it; only TextField and SecureField are shown, other views are ignored.
platformNotes: The web PromptDialog validates (required, maxLength, url and email types, a validate function), shows an error under the field, keeps the dialog open while an async save is pending, has a multiline mode, and offers usePrompt, which returns a promise. The system alert has none of these: it closes when a button is tapped, so check the value afterwards or use a sheet with MonarchTextField, which shows helper and error text. The web's inputType maps to keyboardType, textContentType and textInputAutocapitalization on the TextField. A promise-style call is a withCheckedContinuation around the same state. Android uses AlertDialog with an OutlinedTextField in the same way.
accessibility: System behaviour: the alert confines VoiceOver and keyboard focus, reads the title and message when it appears, and returns focus when it closes.
The TextField title is the placeholder and the spoken name of the field; write it as a label ("Name"), not as an example value.
The button with the cancel role answers the escape gesture.
The alert follows Dynamic Type and scrolls when the message is long.
edgeCases: The text binding keeps its value after the alert closes; reset it before presenting again.
Do not rely on disabling the Save button while the field is empty; treat an empty value as cancel in the action, as the example does.
A second TextField or a SecureField can be added for a name and password; more than two fields belong in a sheet.

name: MonarchProseStyle
title: Prose
wrapsNative: Text with AttributedString (inline Markdown runs styled through an AttributeContainer), a custom Layout with a LayoutValueKey for block spacing, ScrollView(.horizontal) for code blocks
summary: Type styles for long-form content (help articles, release notes, Markdown comments and documents): a base size, a reading measure, the look of each kind of block and the styling of links and code inside text.
whenToUse: When you show content you do not lay out element by element, such as Markdown from a server or a help article, and want the Monarch type scale and rhythm for it.
whenNotToUse: Not for interface text you build with components; use monarchTextStyle(_:) on Text. Not for model output with tables, task lists and footnotes; use MonarchAiMarkdown when it is available. Not for code with copy and wrap controls; use MonarchCodeBlock.
api: struct MonarchProseStyle { init(size: MonarchProseSize = .md, limitsLineLength: Bool = true) }
func inline(_ text: AttributedString, in theme: MonarchTheme) -> AttributedString
func markdown(_ markdown: String, in theme: MonarchTheme) -> AttributedString
func key(_ key: String, in theme: MonarchTheme) -> AttributedString
func highlight(_ text: String, in theme: MonarchTheme) -> AttributedString
struct MonarchProseTable: View { init(columns: [String], rows: [[String]]) }
enum MonarchProseSize { case sm, md, lg }
enum MonarchProseBlock { case paragraph, heading(_ level: Int), listItem(marker: String, depth: Int = 0), quote, code, caption, rule }
struct MonarchProse<Content: View>: View { init(_ style: MonarchProseStyle = MonarchProseStyle(), @ViewBuilder content: () -> Content) }
func monarchProseBlock(_ block: MonarchProseBlock) -> some View

options.name: size
options.description: The base size: sm (14 points) for comments, chat and side panels, md (16 points) for documents, lg (18 points) for long reads. Headings, code and spacing are multiples of it.

options.name: limitsLineLength
options.description: Limits the column to the reading measure, 42 base sizes (672 points at md and the default text size), at the leading edge. Turn it off when the container already sets the width.

options.name: block
options.description: Given to a child of MonarchProse with monarchProseBlock(_:). A child without a kind is a paragraph.

states.name: default
states.description: Prose has no states of its own. Links keep the standard behaviour of Text: they open with the environment's openURL.

appearance: Body text in the default text colour; headings semibold at 1.875, 1.5, 1.25, 1.125 and 1 times the base size; quotations and captions in the muted text colour, quotations after a bar in the strong border colour; code blocks monospaced on the subtle background with the subtle border; thematic breaks in the default border colour; links in the link colour and underlined. Every colour is a theme role, so the dark and high-contrast themes need nothing else.
platformNotes: The parity map named an attribute container for long-form content. An attribute container covers only the inline part: SwiftUI's Text ignores the block intents of AttributedString(markdown:), so it cannot space headings, indent lists and quotations or put code on a panel, and one Text cannot give each heading its header trait. Prose therefore ships the style value (with the inline styling through an AttributeContainer), a column view, MonarchProse, that spaces blocks with the web's rhythm, and the block modifier. The web Prose styles HTML elements by tag; on iOS the renderer (or the app) says which kind each block is. The web's base size is called md here, following the shared size vocabulary. Not offered: tables, images, figures, definition lists, details and keyboard keys inside prose (use Grid, Image, MonarchKbd and DisclosureGroup directly), ProseExclude (a view without monarchProseBlock is a plain paragraph slot and keeps its own styles), and the as parameter (there are no element types). Strong emphasis is drawn bold by SwiftUI, where the web uses semibold.
accessibility: A heading block has the header trait and its heading level (h1 to h6), so the VoiceOver rotor lists the headings.
Links are underlined as well as coloured.
A bullet marker is hidden from VoiceOver; a numbered or lettered marker ("2.", "b)") is read before the item.
The quotation bar and thematic breaks are hidden from VoiceOver.
Every size follows Dynamic Type through a scaled metric relative to body text, and text wraps; code blocks scroll sideways instead.
Code blocks read left to right in a right-to-left layout; everything else follows the layout direction.
edgeCases: Heading levels outside 1 to 6 are clamped.
Long words wrap inside the column; long code lines scroll inside their block.
A child without monarchProseBlock is spaced as a paragraph and keeps its own fonts and colours, apart from the default text colour it inherits.
monarchProseBlock outside MonarchProse uses the default style (md) and adds no spacing.
Text that is not valid Markdown is shown as it is by markdown(_:in:).

options.description: When the value was fetched, checked or computed; shown as relative time.

options.name: systemImage

name: MonarchQueryBuilder
title: QueryBuilder
wrapsNative: Nested VStack groups, each with a segmented Picker for AND / OR; rules stacked vertically with Picker(.menu) for the field and the operator, and a TextField, DatePicker or Picker(.menu) for the value; Buttons with buttonStyle(.monarch()) to add and remove

whenNotToUse: For filters that simply combine with AND, use MonarchFacetedFilterPanel; for a few fixed filters, a Menu with a Picker; for a free-text search, .searchable.

enum MonarchQueryCombinator: String { case and, or }

enum MonarchConditionOperator: String { case equals, notEquals, contains, notContains, greaterThan, atLeast, lessThan, atMost, before, after, isTrue, isFalse, isEmpty, isNotEmpty; var takesValue: Bool }

MonarchQueryBuilderLabels.init(label:group:combinatorBefore:and:or:combinatorLabel:ruleTitle:rule:field:operatorLabel:value:removeRule:addRule:addGroup:removeGroup:emptyGroup:maxDepthReached:maxRulesReached:choose:removedField:chooseDate:operatorName:problem:), every parameter optional

options.name: query
options.description: The top group: a combinator, its rules and its nested groups.

options.name: fields
options.description: The fields a rule can test. The kind (text, number, date, boolean, select) decides the operators and the value input; operators narrows them.

options.name: maxDepth
options.description: How many levels of groups are allowed, counting the top group. 1 turns off nested groups.

options.name: maxRulesPerGroup
options.description: The most rules in one group; Add rule is replaced by a note at the limit.

options.name: showsErrors
options.description: Shows what is missing under each incomplete rule, with a danger border, for example after a save attempt.

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for every built-in string: group names, AND and OR, the spoken names of every control, operator names and problems.

options.name: makeID
options.description: Makes the id of a new rule or group.

states.name: empty group
states.description: "No rules in this group." with Add rule and Add group.

states.name: nested
states.description: A nested group sits inside its parent with a border and a fill that alternates by depth, a header with its name and a remove button.

states.name: deepest level
states.description: Add group is replaced by "Groups cannot be nested any deeper."

states.name: full group
states.description: Add rule is replaced by "A group can have up to 20 rules."

states.name: errors shown
states.description: An incomplete rule has a danger border and a message with an icon: Choose a field, Enter a value, or the chosen value no longer exists.

states.name: removed field
states.description: A rule whose field is no longer in fields shows "amount (removed)" in its field menu.

states.name: no fields
states.description: Add rule and Add group are disabled.

states.name: disabled
states.description: disabled(_:) on the builder disables every menu, field and button and uses the disabled text role.

appearance: Nested groups have a subtle border and alternate the subtle and surface background roles so depth stays visible; rules are surface cards with a subtle border, or the danger strong border when they show a problem. The AND / OR switch and the menus are the system's controls; text uses the default and muted roles. The dark and high-contrast themes swap every role.
platformNotes: Each rule is a MonarchConditionRow, the row of MonarchConditionEditor, so the two components look and speak the same. The web QueryBuilder lays each group's rules out as a ConditionEditor row (field, operator and value side by side) and supports multi-select, tags, in and not-in values. On iOS each rule stacks vertically for a phone, field and operator are menu Pickers, and the value is a text field, a number field that parses in the current locale, a DatePicker (after Choose a date), or a menu of choices; in / not in, multi-select and tags are not offered (use several rules joined by OR). The web's number problem is the value problem here, because a number that does not parse is no number. There is no MonarchConditionEditor yet, so the rule row is part of this component. Focus after removing a group or rule is left to the system. Android builds the same component with the same name.
accessibility: The builder is a container named "Query"; each group is a container named after it ("Top group", "Group 2.1") and its visible name has the header trait.
Each rule is a container named "Top group, rule 1"; its field menu, operator menu and value are named "Top group, rule 1 field", "… operator" and "… value".
The AND / OR switch is a segmented Picker named "Top group combinator", so VoiceOver reads the selected choice.
Remove buttons are icon-only with spoken names ("Remove top group, rule 1", "Remove group 2").
A shown problem is text with an icon, and the rule's hint reads it.
Every control has a touch target of at least 44 points and the text scales with Dynamic Type.
edgeCases: Changing a rule's field resets its operator to the field's first and empties the value; changing the operator keeps the value when it still fits.
A stored operator the field does not offer stays at the top of the operator menu so it is not lost.
A new nested group starts with the opposite combinator of its parent.
matches(_:calendar:) treats an empty group as matching, compares text without case and dates by day in the given calendar; the server stays the authority.
A number field keeps what is typed while it is not a number and stores nil until it parses.

whenToUse: In an app with many named places that people know by name (conversations, projects, documents, people), as the fastest way to move between them.
whenNotToUse: For running actions such as “Create issue”, use the command-palette recipe. For filtering one list on screen, use searchable on that screen.

appearance: The sheet, navigation bar and search field are the system's in every theme; rows are MonarchSearchResultItem rows with the place's symbol, the highlighted title and an optional second line in the muted colour.
platformNotes: The web QuickSwitcher is a preset of CommandPalette: a centred dialog with a Mod+K hotkey, recent items, forgiving matching, debounced remote sources and a “Search for” row. On iOS it is the command-palette recipe with those defaults: a sheet is the phone's surface for a modal task, searchable gives the system field with dictation and the Search key, keyboardShortcut gives Command-K on a hardware keyboard. Remote sources are the app's own task(id: query) that sets the results and isLoading; Monarch adds no networking, debounce or cancellation helpers. There is no Android entry yet.
accessibility: The trigger is a MonarchButton with a 44-point target; the Command-K shortcut is listed in the iPad keyboard shortcut overlay.
The sheet has a Close button in the cancellation position and can be dismissed by swipe or the VoiceOver escape gesture.
Each place is a button read with its title and second line; group headings, including Recent, have the header trait and are read with their count.
The results summary is announced when the query changes, as MonarchSearchResults does.
edgeCases: Clear the query in onDismiss so every opening starts with the recent places.
Navigate after the sheet has dismissed when the destination presents another sheet.
Letter-order matching finds more than word matching: rank whole-word matches first when lists are long.
Debounce remote searches in the app's task(id:) and drop results for an older query.

name: MonarchRangeSlider
title: RangeSlider
wrapsNative: GeometryReader with Capsule and Circle shapes, DragGesture, and accessibilityAdjustableAction on each thumb
summary: A track with two thumbs that chooses a lower and an upper value; the thumbs never cross.
whenToUse: For a filter or setting with a lower and an upper bound on one scale: a price, a salary or an age band, working hours.
whenNotToUse: For one value, use the system Slider. For exact amounts people type, use two MonarchNumberInput fields. For dates, use a date range picker.
api: init(_ label: String, value: Binding<ClosedRange<Double>>, in bounds: ClosedRange<Double> = 0...100, step: Double = 1, minimumStepsBetween: Int = 0, size: MonarchRangeSliderSize = .md, isInvalid: Bool = false, labels: MonarchRangeSliderLabels = MonarchRangeSliderLabels(), valueText: ((Double) -> String)? = nil, showsValue: Bool = false, onEditingChanged: @escaping (Bool) -> Void = { _ in })
enum MonarchRangeSliderSize { case sm, md }
struct MonarchRangeSliderLabels { init(minimum: String? = nil, maximum: String? = nil, range: (@Sendable (String, String) -> String)? = nil) }

options.name: label
options.description: What the range is. Spoken with each thumb ("Price, Minimum"); not drawn. Give the visible label with MonarchFormField.

options.name: value
options.description: The lower and upper values.

options.name: bounds
options.description: The lowest and highest values.

options.name: step
options.description: The distance between allowed values. 0 allows any value.

options.name: minimumStepsBetween
options.description: The smallest gap between the thumbs, in steps. With 0 the thumbs may meet.

options.name: size
options.description: The thickness of the track and the size of the thumbs. The touch area is 44 points high at both sizes.

options.name: isInvalid
options.description: Draws the range and the thumb borders in the danger colour.

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for "Minimum", "Maximum" and the "20 – 80" range text.

options.name: valueText
options.description: Formats a value for VoiceOver and the shown range. The number in the current locale by default.

options.name: showsValue
options.description: Shows the formatted range above the track.

options.name: onEditingChanged
options.description: Runs with true when a drag starts and false when it ends, like Slider. Save the value on false.

states.name: default
states.description: The track in the emphasis background, the range between the thumbs in the accent colour, thumbs on the surface colour with an accent border.

states.name: thumbs together
states.description: Both thumbs at one value; dragging or adjusting can only move them apart.

states.name: dragging
states.description: The thumb picked when the touch started follows the finger and stops at the other thumb; onEditingChanged(true) at the start and onEditingChanged(false) at the end.

states.name: invalid
states.description: The range and the thumb borders take the solid danger colour.

states.name: disabled
states.description: Set with disabled(_:). Muted track, range and thumbs in the disabled colours; touches and VoiceOver adjustments do nothing.

appearance: The track uses the emphasis background, the range the solid accent colour of the theme (solid danger when invalid), the thumbs the surface colour with a two-point border in the range colour. The shown range uses the caption style in the muted text colour with tabular digits. All are theme roles, so dark and high-contrast themes follow.
platformNotes: SwiftUI has no two-thumb slider, so this is drawn: the plan's build coverage is right. Android styles a RangeSlider in its theme instead. The web's marks (labelled ticks under the track), largeStep (Page Up and Page Down), name (hidden form inputs) and the separate onValueChange and onValueCommit callbacks are not offered: the binding changes on every move, and onEditingChanged marks the end of a drag as on Slider. The web's accent tone is used directly through the accent colour roles, because MonarchTone has no accent case. The value is a ClosedRange<Double> rather than a generic BinaryFloatingPoint value. The thumbs are not focusable with a hardware keyboard; VoiceOver and Switch Control use the adjustable action.
accessibility: Each thumb is its own adjustable element, labelled with the label and "Minimum" or "Maximum" ("Price, Minimum"); the name is built by a tested pure function and can be replaced with labels.
The value of each thumb is the formatted number from valueText.
Swiping up or down on a thumb moves it by one step (a hundredth of the bounds when step is 0) and stops at the other thumb plus the gap.
The lower thumb is read before the upper thumb in both layout directions (accessibilitySortPriority).
The shown range and the track are hidden from VoiceOver, because the thumbs carry the same values.
Each thumb and the track have a touch area 44 points high.
edgeCases: A value outside the bounds or off the step grid is drawn snapped; the binding is only written when a thumb moves.
When both thumbs sit at the maximum, a touch there picks the lower thumb so it can be pulled back.
In right-to-left layouts the lower value is on the right. Positions are computed in reading order by a tested function and the drawing is kept left to right so it is not mirrored twice.
A gap wider than the bounds is reduced to the width of the bounds.

summary: A "View receipt" button that opens an expense's receipt in Quick Look, running the app's loader for a private file only when pressed, with a loading state, Try again and a "No receipt" fallback.
whenToUse: On an expense, bill or reimbursement line with an attached receipt or invoice scan, especially when the file is private and must be fetched with the app's authorised request only when someone opens it.
whenNotToUse: For uploading a receipt, use PhotosPicker or fileImporter. For browsing many documents, use a list with quickLookPreview(_:in:). For a file that is not a receipt, use quickLookPreview(_:) directly (see file-preview).

appearance: The button is a Monarch ghost button at the small size by default; the error uses the inline error retry's danger roles; "No receipt" is caption text in the muted text colour. Quick Look is drawn by the system. Colours come from theme roles in every theme.
platformNotes: The web ReceiptPreview opens images in a dialog with Download, PDFs in a new tab or an embedded viewer, and explains formats the browser cannot draw (HEIC). On iOS Quick Look draws images including HEIC, PDFs and most documents and has its own share action, so there is no dialog, Download button, pdf option or unsupported-format messages; open, onOpenChange and onLoadError are replaced by the loader's thrown error and onClose. The loader must return a local file: Quick Look cannot show a remote URL, and Monarch does not download. Android ships the same MonarchReceiptPreview.
accessibility: The button is a standard MonarchButton labelled "View receipt"; while loading it is read as "Loading receipt".
A failed load is announced with the error text, and Try again is a separate button.
"No receipt" is plain text, not a disabled button.
Quick Look provides its own VoiceOver support for the file.
The button keeps a 44-point touch target at every size.
edgeCases: Pressing again while loading starts a new load and cancels the previous one.
Leaving the screen while loading cancels the loader's task; the loader should respect cancellation.
A URL that is not a file URL counts as no receipt; fetch it in load instead.
Quick Look presentation and onClose were checked only by compiling and unit tests of the close rule; they were not tried on a device.

Many badges wrap onto new lines in MonarchFlowLayout.
On the first and last record the previous and next buttons are disabled.

The web overlay is translucent; the iOS solid variant is opaque, because colours come from roles and are not dimmed. Strings are replaced through one labels value instead of a messages object. If the view is removed from the layout while not recording, the start and the stop are not announced.

appearance: Codes sit on a panel with the subtle background and subtle border roles, in the code type role. Buttons are Monarch buttons: ghost for show and hide, secondary for copy and save, danger for regenerate, primary for Continue. All colours are theme roles, so dark and high-contrast themes follow.
platformNotes: The web's Download becomes "Save or share": a ShareLink with a plain-text file, from which the person can save to Files, a password manager or another app. The web's confirm dialog is the system confirmationDialog. Revealed state is internal (startsRevealed) rather than controlled. The web's formatRecoveryCodes helper is the heading parameter; a fully custom format is not offered. Several closures are optional (onRegenerate, onAcknowledge). Pass each one with its label: Swift gives a single unlabelled trailing closure to the first parameter that accepts it, which is onRegenerate.

A used code has the value "Used", so its state does not depend on the strike-through.

New codes are announced after regenerating.
A missing acknowledgement is shown with an icon and text and announced.
edgeCases: The grid has as many columns as fit at 112 points each, scaled with Dynamic Type, so the largest text sizes show one column.
A new set of codes clears the acknowledgement; marking a code used does not.
The codes can be selected as text for manual copying.

platformNotes: The built-in lists are the web's: US, CA, AU, GB and IN with English names. The text field tells AutoFill it holds the state or region of an address.
edgeCases: Changing the country resets the field; the app clears selection itself if it should not carry over.
Supplied and loaded regions keep their order; the built-in lists are in alphabetical order of their English names, as on the web.
A loader that returns [] gives a text field, unless allowsTextEntry is off.
A failed loader is asked again only after Try again.

summary: A recipe, not a component: remove a member from a workspace after handing over their open work to other members (all at once or per kind of work), confirm in a system confirmation dialog, then offer Undo in a toast.
whenToUse: When an admin removes someone who may still own open work: issues, reviews, documents or deals that would otherwise be left without an owner.
whenNotToUse: For someone who owns nothing, MonarchMemberRow's own remove confirmation or a confirmationDialog is enough. For a member leaving on their own, use the leave-workspace-flow recipe. For many members at once, use the bulk-destructive-flow recipe.

states.description: Shown only when the member owns open work: one MonarchAssigneePicker for all of it and a toggle to choose a person for each kind of work instead; the consequence list below says where each kind goes.

states.name: per item
states.description: One MonarchAssigneePicker per kind of work, labelled with its count, each starting from the all-at-once choice.

states.name: confirm
states.description: Remove in the navigation bar opens a system confirmation dialog titled Remove <name>? with a destructive Remove member button and Cancel.

states.name: removing
states.description: Remove is replaced by a progress indicator, Cancel is disabled and the sheet cannot be swiped away.

states.name: failed
states.description: A danger MonarchInlineNotice below the consequences; the sheet stays open with the choices kept.

states.name: removed
states.description: The sheet closes and a toast says the member was removed, with Undo.

appearance: A system sheet with a navigation bar holding Cancel and a destructive Remove; Monarch's member row, assignee pickers, consequence list with its kind colours and inline notice on the canvas background. The confirmation dialog is the system action sheet and the toast uses Monarch's toast host. Every colour is a theme role, so dark and both high-contrast themes follow.
platformNotes: The web RemoveMemberFlow is one component on a WizardDialog with a reassign step and a confirm step, a step-up authentication option, number formatting and a useUndoToast bridge. Android composes a recipe with the same states in a ModalBottomSheet with two steps and a Material 3 snackbar. On iOS the recipe follows the system pattern for a destructive action in a sheet: the hand-over and the consequences share one screen in a NavigationStack, Cancel and Remove sit in the navigation bar, and the final step is a system confirmationDialog with a destructive button instead of a second in-sheet step; Undo is MonarchToastCenter's toast. The per-item choice is a native Toggle where Android uses MonarchCheckboxRow. The app writes plural strings with its String Catalog, runs re-authentication (for example MonarchStepUpAuthDialog in a nested sheet) before the removal, and sends the reassignments to its server.
accessibility: The navigation title names the member, and Hand over their open work is a heading (header trait).
Each MonarchAssigneePicker is named by its label: Reassign all open work to, or the count and kind of work.
MonarchConsequenceList reads each consequence with its kind, so where the work goes does not depend on colour.
Remove has the destructive role, and the confirmation dialog's Remove member button is read as destructive by VoiceOver.
While removing, the progress indicator in the navigation bar reads Removing <name>, and Cancel is read as dimmed.
The toast host announces the toast, and Undo is reachable with VoiceOver.
edgeCases: When the member owns nothing, leave out the hand-over section: the sheet shows the member row and the consequences only.
Leave the removed member, and the assign-to-me shortcut, out of the people offered in the pickers.
Turning on per item copies the all-at-once choice into each picker, so nothing is lost.
Reset the choices and any error each time the sheet opens.
If the removal fails, keep the choices and show the error with MonarchInlineNotice; the sheet stays open.
Long names wrap in the member row and the consequence list; the navigation title truncates, and the confirmation dialog repeats the full name.

summary: What renews or expires next: one row per renewal with its date and day count, amount, status, owner and next step, with filters, totals per currency and a row action.
whenToUse: On a billing, contracts or assets screen where people work through upcoming renewals: what is due, for how much, who owns it and what happens next.
whenNotToUse: For active recurring subscriptions with their monthly figure use MonarchSubscriptionsTable. For the cost of unused items use MonarchSavingsPanel.

appearance: A MonarchSectionCard. Rows have the name in the strong body style with the amount at the trailing edge (stacked under it when it does not fit), the date in the label style, captions in the muted text colour, a small MonarchStatusBadge and a secondary Update button. Totals are captions over subheading MonarchMoney figures. All colours are theme roles, so light, dark and both high-contrast themes follow.
platformNotes: The web shows a table with Item, Renewal, Amount, Owner and Status columns that drops columns on narrow screens; on iOS every renewal is a stacked row with the same facts, the phone pattern for a list with a detail screen (onSelect). The web's filters are a SegmentedControl; here a segmented Picker that falls back to a menu Picker when the options do not fit. The web's filterControls slot is left to the app (put extra controls above the panel), its href and renderLink become onSelect, its minorUnits flag is not offered (pass major units as Decimal, as MonarchMoney does) and its custom empty node is the labels' empty title and message. The web's headingLevel has no iOS equivalent. Android builds the same component; the iOS API uses a filter binding where Android passes selectedFilter with onFilterChange. Several closures are optional (onRetry, onSelect, onAction, canAct). Pass each one with its label: Swift gives a single unlabelled trailing closure to the first parameter that accepts it, which is onRetry.
accessibility: The title has the header trait (from MonarchSectionCard).

Each renewal is one element whose label is its name and whose value is built by a tested pure function: description, Due soon when urgent, date and day count, amount, status, probability, renewal note, owner and next step, outcome.
With onSelect the renewal is a button; the chevron is decorative.
The row action is a separate MonarchButton with a 44-point target, named "Update <name>".
Statuses have words and icons, urgency has an icon and the spoken Due soon, and overdue steps start with the word Overdue, so nothing depends on colour.
Each total is one element; the totals group is named Totals by currency.
edgeCases: A renewal without a date reads Unknown date and has no day count.
A notice deadline replaces the day count.
daysUntil from the server wins over the count worked out from now.
Days are counted between calendar days in the calendar's time zone, so a renewal later today is "today".
An unknown status key shows the neutral unknown look with a readable label made from the key.

whenNotToUse: For tiles in two dimensions, use MonarchSortableGrid. For moving items between columns, use a Kanban board.

EditButton()

AccessibilityNotification.Announcement(_ string: String).post()

platformNotes: The web ReorderableList draws its own handles, offers optional move buttons and announces every step in a live region. On iOS the system list already has a reorder control in edit mode, so Monarch ships no type; the recipe adds Move up and Move down accessibility actions that announce the new position. Android builds MonarchReorderableList because Compose has no built-in list reordering.
accessibility: The reorder control is the system's, with its own VoiceOver support in edit mode.
The recipe adds Move up and Move down accessibility actions to each row, so VoiceOver and Switch Control can move a row one place without a drag.
After each action the recipe posts an announcement with the new position: "Contacted moved to position 1 of 4".
Each row is one element with accessibilityElement(children: .combine).
edgeCases: EditButton and \.editMode exist only on iOS; the example guards them with #if os(iOS) so it also builds on the macOS host.
onMove gives a destination offset in the list before removal, which Array.move(fromOffsets:toOffset:) expects.
The Move up action on the first row and Move down on the last row do nothing.

name: MonarchResizablePanels
title: ResizablePanels
wrapsNative: GeometryReader, HStackLayout and VStackLayout, DragGesture, focusable with onKeyPress, accessibilityAdjustableAction
summary: Two panels, side by side or stacked, with a separator the person drags, or moves from a keyboard or with VoiceOver, to resize them.
whenToUse: On an iPad or another regular-width screen, when two panes stay on screen together and people choose how much space each gets: a list beside a preview, an editor above its output.
whenNotToUse: For a list and a detail that become one pane with a back button on a phone, use NavigationSplitView (see split-layout). On a phone in portrait there is rarely room for two panes; the default stacks them.
api: MonarchResizablePanels.init(fraction: Binding<Double>, axis: MonarchResizablePanelsAxis = .horizontal, range: ClosedRange<Double> = 0.1...0.9, step: Double = 0.05, showsGrip: Bool = false, handleLabel: String? = nil, stacksWhenCompact: Bool = true, collapsesFirst: Bool = false, onResizeEnded: (@MainActor (Double) -> Void)? = nil, @ViewBuilder first: () -> First, @ViewBuilder second: () -> Second)
enum MonarchResizablePanelsAxis { case horizontal, vertical }

options.name: fraction
options.description: The share of the first panel, from 0 to 1. The app owns it; keep it in @SceneStorage or @AppStorage to restore the layout.

options.name: axis
options.description: horizontal: side by side, the first panel at the leading edge. vertical: stacked, the first panel on top.

options.name: range
options.description: The smallest and largest share of the first panel. Limited to 0...1.

options.name: step
options.description: The share one arrow key press or one VoiceOver swipe moves the separator.

options.name: showsGrip
options.description: Whether a grip is drawn in the middle of the separator.

options.name: handleLabel
options.description: Replaces the built-in spoken name "Resize panels".

options.name: stacksWhenCompact
options.description: Whether side-by-side panels are stacked at their natural height, with a plain divider and no resizing, when the horizontal size class is compact.

options.name: onResizeEnded
options.description: Called with the share when a drag ends and after each keyboard or VoiceOver step. Save the layout here.

options.name: first
options.description: The leading or top panel.

options.name: second
options.description: The trailing or bottom panel.

states.name: resting
states.description: A hairline separator in the strong border colour between the panels.

states.name: dragging
states.description: The separator and the grip take the accent colour and the line is 2 points thick. The panels resize as the finger moves.

states.name: focused
states.description: With a hardware keyboard the separator takes focus and looks as it does while dragged.

states.name: disabled
states.description: The separator uses the subtle border colour and does not respond to a drag, the keyboard or VoiceOver. Set with disabled(_:).

states.name: stacked
states.description: At a compact width with stacksWhenCompact, the panels are one above the other at their natural height with a MonarchDivider between them.

appearance: A 1-point line in the strong border role; the accent role and 2 points while dragged or focused; the subtle border role when disabled. The optional grip is a capsule in the same colour. The panels draw their own backgrounds.
platformNotes: The parity map named NavigationSplitView column widths for this entry. On iOS navigationSplitViewColumnWidth only proposes a width and the person cannot drag the column edge, so the separator is custom in every case. The web takes any number of panels with alternating handles and sizes in percent; iOS takes two panels and one share from 0 to 1, and a third pane is a MonarchResizablePanels nested in a panel. The web keeps the sizes itself (defaultSizes, onLayout); here the app owns the binding and onResizeEnded is the moment to save. Not offered: collapsible panels (collapsedSize, Enter to collapse) and a per-handle disabled flag (disable the whole view). The web stacks below 768 pixels only when stackOnNarrow is set; here stacking at a compact width is the default, because two resizable columns do not fit a phone in portrait. Android ships the same two-panel API.
accessibility: The separator is one element named "Resize panels" or by handleLabel.
Its value is the share of the first panel as a whole percentage, for example "40%".
It has the adjustable action: swiping up or down with VoiceOver moves it by step.

With a hardware keyboard the separator is focusable. The arrow keys along the axis move it by step in the direction they point, so left and right swap in a right-to-left layout. Home and End move it to the ends of range.
The touch target is 44 points across, centred on the line, and overlaps the edges of both panels.
Dragging follows the layout direction: in a right-to-left layout the first panel is on the right.
The active state is a thicker line as well as the accent colour.
The panels are not animated while they resize, so there is nothing for Reduce Motion to turn off; the colour change of the line is not animated when Reduce Motion is on.
edgeCases: The view fills the space it is offered. Inside a ScrollView give it a height.
A fraction outside range is shown at the nearest end of the range; the binding is not rewritten until the person moves the separator.
The content of a panel is clipped to the panel.
Controls within 22 points of the separator share their touch area with it; the separator wins.
When stacked, fraction, range and step have no effect and no separator is offered.
The vertical axis never stacks.

title: ResponsiveDialog
wrapsNative: sheet(isPresented:onDismiss:content:), which is a sheet from the bottom at compact width and a centred form sheet at regular width, with presentationDetents for the phone and a NavigationStack toolbar for the actions
summary: A dialog that is a centred panel on a large screen and a bottom sheet on a phone is the standard SwiftUI sheet, which adapts to the window size by itself. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: For a short task or form that should be a centred dialog on an iPad and a sheet on an iPhone: editing a record, inviting a person, choosing export options.
whenNotToUse: For a message with one or two buttons use alert (see dialog). For a long, multi-screen task use a pushed screen or fullScreenCover.
api: func sheet(isPresented: Binding<Bool>, onDismiss: (() -> Void)? = nil, content: () -> some View) -> some View
func presentationDetents(_ detents: Set<PresentationDetent>) -> some View
func presentationDragIndicator(_ visibility: Visibility) -> some View
func interactiveDismissDisabled(_ isDisabled: Bool = true) -> some View

states.name: compact width
states.description: A sheet from the bottom at the detents given, with a drag indicator.

states.name: regular width
states.description: A form sheet centred over a dimmed screen; detents are not used.

states.name: guarded
states.description: With interactiveDismissDisabled the sheet cannot be swiped away (see unsaved-changes-guard).

appearance: The system draws the sheet and its dimming. presentationBackground with the theme's surface colour and Monarch components inside make it match the theme in light, dark and both high-contrast themes.
platformNotes: The web ResponsiveDialog switches from Dialog to a bottom sheet below a breakpoint (sheetBelow) and shows a grab handle. The iOS sheet already does this by size class: there is no breakpoint to set, and handle is presentationDragIndicator. On iOS 18 and later presentationSizing(.form) or (.page) chooses the size at regular width; Monarch supports iOS 17, so the system default form sheet is used. Android builds a MonarchResponsiveDialog because Compose has no adaptive sheet.
accessibility: System behaviour: the sheet is modal at every size, VoiceOver focus moves into it and returns to the presenting control when it closes, and the escape gesture dismisses it unless dismissal is disabled.
Give the content a title in a NavigationStack (navigationTitle), which VoiceOver reads first.
Put Cancel and the main action in the toolbar with the cancellationAction and confirmationAction placements, so their roles are clear.
edgeCases: At the largest text sizes the medium detent may be too short; include .large.
Detents apply only at compact width; test both widths.
Do not nest a second sheet for a confirmation inside the sheet; use an alert or confirmationDialog.

summary: A recipe, not a component: confirm revoking an API key, an OAuth client, portal access, sessions or devices, listing what is revoked, when it was last used and what happens, with optional type-to-confirm and re-authentication.
whenToUse: Behind every Revoke, Sign out or Remove action on keys, connected apps, sessions, devices or someone's portal access.
whenNotToUse: For a device list with its own simple confirmation, MonarchDeviceList's built-in alert is enough. For leaving a workspace yourself, use the leave workspace recipe.

Text(lastUsed.formatted(.relative(presentation: .named)))
MonarchConsequenceList([MonarchConsequence(.removed, "…"), MonarchConsequence(.warning, "…")], heading: "What happens")
MonarchTypeToConfirmInput(phrase: keyName, text: $phrase)
MonarchButton("Revoke key", variant: .danger, isLoading: isRevoking, fullWidth: true) { … }

states.description: The question naming what is revoked, a line on what it means, the item with its prefix and last-used time, the consequences, and a danger button naming the action.

states.name: type to confirm
states.description: For keys and OAuth clients, the danger button stays disabled until the name is typed exactly.

states.name: step-up

platformNotes: The web's RevokeAccessFlow is one component with built-in copy for five kinds (api-key, oauth-client, portal-access, session, device) and plural forms. On iOS it is a recipe: the copy is the app's, written for its kind and count, and the step is a sheet because a system alert cannot hold a list, a text field with a match check, or a pending state. Danger is the default for keys and OAuth clients (they cannot be undone); for sessions, devices and portal access, which can sign in again, use a plain confirmation alert or the same sheet with warning wording. The web's stepUp prop is the second sheet with MonarchStepUpAuthDialog. Android composes the same recipe.

MonarchConsequenceList reads each consequence with its kind.
MonarchTypeToConfirmInput announces when the typed name matches.
The row's Revoke button is named with the item ("Revoke CI deploy key").
Buttons are MonarchButtons with 44-point touch targets and a busy state while revoking; the sheet cannot be dismissed while revoking.
edgeCases: For several items, list each one and put the count in the title and the button ("Revoke 3 keys").
An item never used reads "Never used" instead of a time.
Reset the typed phrase each time the sheet opens.
