title: SearchInput
wrapsNative: searchable(text:placement:prompt:) in a NavigationStack, with onSubmit(of: .search), searchSuggestions and searchScopes
summary: A search box for filtering a list or querying a server is the system search field, added to the navigation bar with searchable. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: To search or filter the content of a screen that has a navigation bar. The system supplies the magnifier, the clear button, the Cancel button, the keyboard's Search key and the hide-on-scroll behaviour.
whenNotToUse: Not for a search box in the middle of a screen, inside a form or a sheet without a navigation bar: use MonarchTextField there. Not for choosing one value from a list (use a Picker).
api: func searchable(text: Binding<String>, placement: SearchFieldPlacement = .automatic, prompt: String) -> some View
func onSubmit(of triggers: SubmitTriggers, _ action: @escaping () -> Void) -> some View
func searchSuggestions<S: View>(_ suggestions: () -> S) -> some View
func searchScopes<V: Hashable, S: View>(_ scope: Binding<V>, scopes: () -> S) -> some View

states.name: empty
states.description: The magnifier and the prompt.

states.name: active
states.description: The field has focus, the keyboard is open and the system shows a Cancel button. isSearching in the environment is true.

states.name: with text
states.description: The system shows a clear button at the trailing edge.

states.name: loading
states.description: The field has no pending state. Show a ProgressView in the results while a server query runs.

appearance: The system draws the field in every theme. The theme's tint colours the cursor and the Cancel button; Monarch colours and type are not applied to the field.
platformNotes: The web SearchInput draws an icon, a clear button, a pending spinner and a shortcut hint, and debounces onSearch. On iOS the icon, clear button and Cancel are the system's. The web's debounce is task(id: query) with a short sleep, as in the second example; pending is a ProgressView in the results; the shortcut hint is not shown. The web's sizes do not apply. MonarchTextField has no leading icon or clear button yet, so an inline search box outside a navigation bar is a plain labelled field. Android styles the Material 3 SearchBar as MonarchSearchBar; iOS adopts the system field.
accessibility: System behaviour: the field has the search field trait, the prompt as its placeholder and a labelled clear button.
System behaviour: the keyboard's return key is Search, and onSubmit(of: .search) runs on it.
Announce the number of results after a query with AccessibilityNotification.Announcement, since the list changes without focus moving.
The field follows Dynamic Type.
edgeCases: searchable has no effect without a NavigationStack or NavigationSplitView around the view.
placement .navigationBarDrawer(displayMode: .always) keeps the field visible; the default hides it until the list is pulled down.
Filtering on every keystroke is fine for local data; debounce a server query.
An empty result needs its own message: ContentUnavailableView.search.

name: MonarchSearchResultItem
title: SearchResultItem
wrapsNative: Button with a ButtonStyle, Text with a highlighted AttributedString, MonarchFileTypeIcon, MonarchFlowLayout
summary: One search result: a title, a breadcrumb path, a snippet with the matched words highlighted, an optional leading icon and optional trailing details.
whenToUse: For each row of a search results list or a global search panel.
whenNotToUse: Not for search suggestions while typing; use the system searchSuggestions modifier. Not for plain navigation rows without a query; use a List row or LabeledContent.
api: init(_ title: String, path: [String] = [], snippet: String? = nil, terms: [String] = [], titleRanges: [Range<Int>]? = nil, snippetRanges: [Range<Int>]? = nil, snippetHasMarkTags: Bool = false, systemImage: String? = nil, fileName: String? = nil, pathLabel: String? = nil, action: (@MainActor () -> Void)? = nil, @ViewBuilder meta: () -> Meta)

init(_ title: String, path: [String] = [], snippet: String? = nil, terms: [String] = [], titleRanges: [Range<Int>]? = nil, snippetRanges: [Range<Int>]? = nil, snippetHasMarkTags: Bool = false, systemImage: String? = nil, fileName: String? = nil, pathLabel: String? = nil, action: (@MainActor () -> Void)? = nil) where Meta == EmptyView
static func terms(from query: String) -> [String] where Meta == EmptyView

options.name: title
options.description: The title, as plain text.

options.name: path
options.description: Breadcrumb segments, shown with a slash between them and read as a list.

options.name: snippet
options.description: A short excerpt of the matching content, at most three lines.

options.name: terms
options.description: Words to highlight in the title and snippet, matched without regard to case. Use terms(from:).

options.name: titleRanges
options.description: Exact matches in the title as UTF-16 offsets, as the web and most search services count. Replaces terms for the title.

options.name: snippetRanges
options.description: Exact matches in the snippet as UTF-16 offsets. Replaces terms for the snippet.

options.name: snippetHasMarkTags
options.description: The snippet carries <mark> and </mark> markers, for example from PostgreSQL ts_headline. Only those markers are read.

options.name: systemImage
options.description: An SF Symbol in the leading tile.

options.name: fileName
options.description: A file name; its file type icon fills the leading tile. Takes precedence over systemImage.

options.name: pathLabel
options.description: Replaces the built-in Location read before the path.

options.name: action
options.description: Runs when the row is activated. With it the row is a Button and the title takes the link colour.

options.name: meta
options.description: Trailing details such as a badge, a date or an owner.

states.name: interactive
states.description: With an action: the title is in the link colour and the row shows a subtle fill while pressed.

states.name: plain
states.description: Without an action: the title is in the default text colour and the row is static content.

states.name: disabled
states.description: With .disabled(true) the row does not respond; the system dims the button.

appearance: The title is medium weight in the link colour (or the default text colour), the path and meta are captions in the muted text colour with subtle separators, and the snippet is muted body text. Matched words have the subtle warning fill, the default text colour and a semibold weight. The leading tile is the muted background with a muted icon.
platformNotes: The web item renders the title as a link (href) or a button and supports a router link component and roving tab index. On iOS the row runs an action; to navigate, leave the action out and wrap the row in a NavigationLink, or open a URL in the action. Exact ranges use UTF-16 offsets, the same numbers the web receives. The web places the meta under the text on narrow screens; on iOS it moves under the text at the accessibility text sizes. The match fill has no padding or rounded corner, which AttributedString cannot draw.
accessibility: The row is one element that reads the title, then Location and the path segments separated by commas, then the snippet without markers, then the meta.
With an action the row is a Button, so it has the button trait and one activation.
Matches are also semibold, so they do not depend on the fill colour; the highlight itself is not read.
The leading icon is decorative.
An interactive row is at least 44 points high; text wraps and scales with Dynamic Type.
edgeCases: Text is never parsed as markup: only <mark> and </mark> are read, and only when snippetHasMarkTags is true; other tags stay visible text.
Ranges outside the text are clamped, overlapping ranges merge, and an offset inside a character covers the whole character.
The snippet is limited to three lines; the title wraps without a limit.
Empty path segments are skipped.

name: MonarchSearchResults
title: SearchResults
wrapsNative: List with .listStyle(.plain) and a Section per group, rows of MonarchSearchResultItem; MonarchErrorState, MonarchEmptyState and redacted(reason: .placeholder) skeleton rows for the states
summary: Search results in labelled groups with counts, highlighted matches, a summary that is announced, Show all buttons, and loading, empty and error states.
whenToUse: As the content of a search screen, usually with .searchable, when results come back in groups (documents, people, projects) or as one list.
whenNotToUse: For suggestions while typing, use .searchSuggestions. For one result row elsewhere, use MonarchSearchResultItem.
api: init(groups: [MonarchSearchResultGroup], query: String = "", isLoading: Bool = false, isFailed: Bool = false, errorMessage: String? = nil, loadingRows: Int = 4, labels: MonarchSearchResultsLabels = MonarchSearchResultsLabels(), onRetry: (@MainActor () -> Void)? = nil, onShowAll: (@MainActor (MonarchSearchResultGroup) -> Void)? = nil, onSelect: @escaping @MainActor (MonarchSearchResult, MonarchSearchResultGroup) -> Void)
struct MonarchSearchResultGroup: Identifiable { init(_ title: String?, id: String, results: [MonarchSearchResult], total: Int? = nil, systemImage: String? = nil) }

struct MonarchSearchResult: Identifiable { init(_ title: String, id: String, path: [String] = [], snippet: String? = nil, titleRanges: [Range<Int>]? = nil, snippetRanges: [Range<Int>]? = nil, snippetHasMarkTags: Bool = false, systemImage: String? = nil, fileName: String? = nil, meta: String? = nil) }

struct MonarchSearchResultsLabels { var summary: ((Int, String) -> String)?; var loading: String?; var emptyTitle: ((String) -> String)?; var emptyMessage, errorTitle, retry: String?; var showAll: ((String?, Int) -> String)?; var groupCount: ((Int) -> String)? }

options.name: groups
options.description: Results in groups; a group with a nil title has no heading, for results without groups. Empty groups are left out.

options.name: query
options.description: What the person searched for: its words are highlighted and it is named in the summary and empty title.

options.name: isLoading
options.description: A search is running: skeleton rows when there are no results yet, otherwise the results stay and the summary reads Searching….

options.name: isFailed
options.description: The search failed: an error state replaces the results.

options.name: errorMessage
options.description: The reason, shown under Search failed.

options.name: loadingRows
options.description: Skeleton rows while loading with no results.

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for every built-in string; counted strings are closures.

options.name: onRetry
options.description: Adds Try again to the error state.

options.name: onShowAll
options.description: Adds "Show all 24 in Documents" after a group whose total is larger than its results.

options.name: onSelect
options.description: Opens a result.

states.name: ready
states.description: The summary line, then the groups with headings, counts and highlighted rows.

states.name: refreshing
states.description: Results stay, the summary reads Searching… with a small spinner.

states.name: loading
states.description: Redacted skeleton rows, hidden from VoiceOver.

states.name: empty
states.description: MonarchEmptyState (filtered kind) with "No results for “query”" and a hint.

states.name: error
states.description: MonarchErrorState with Search failed, the message and Try again.

appearance: The summary and counts in the muted text role, headings in the default text role, counts on a muted capsule, rows from MonarchSearchResultItem with matches on the subtle warning fill. The list background is cleared so the screen's canvas shows, in light, dark and both high-contrast themes.
platformNotes: The web results are one Tab stop with arrow-key navigation; on iOS each result is a button in a List and VoiceOver moves through them in order, with the Headings rotor on group headings. The web's heading level and custom empty node are not offered; the web's linkComponent and href become onSelect. The web shows results without groups when given results instead of groups; here pass one group with a nil title. Android has the same parameters. Several closures are optional (onRetry, onShowAll). Pass each one with its label: Swift gives a single unlabelled trailing closure to the first parameter that accepts it, which is onRetry.
accessibility: The summary is announced when it changes (results count, Searching…, or the empty title), as the web's live region; Search failed is announced when the search fails.
Group headings have the header trait and are read with their count, such as "Documents, 24 results"; the icon is decorative.
Each result is a button read as title, location path, snippet and meta (from MonarchSearchResultItem).
Skeleton rows are hidden from VoiceOver.
The empty and error states keep their own accessibility (header titles, retry button).
Rows are at least 44 points tall and text scales with Dynamic Type.
edgeCases: A total smaller than the results shown is raised to the number shown.
An error wins over results and loading; results win over loading.
A query of only spaces is treated as no query in the summary and empty title.
The List scrolls itself, so do not put the results inside another ScrollView; give the screen the full height.

name: MonarchSecretField
title: SecretField
wrapsNative: SecureField, swapped for TextField while revealed, with .privacySensitive(); UIPasteboard.setItems(_:options:) with .localOnly for copy
summary: A masked secret (API key, token, signing secret) with a reveal toggle, an optional copy button and a "set, not shown" state, over the standard SecureField and TextField.
whenToUse: When a settings screen takes or shows a credential for an integration, when a newly created key is shown once to be copied, or when the server holds a saved secret and the user may replace it.
whenNotToUse: For a sign-in password use MonarchPasswordInput, which offers saved passwords. For a value that is not sensitive use MonarchCopyField or MonarchTextField.
api: init(_ label: String, text: Binding<String>, prompt: String? = nil, helper: String? = nil, error: String? = nil, isSet: Bool = false, isRevealable: Bool = true, isCopyable: Bool = false, isReadOnly: Bool = false, isRevealed: Binding<Bool>? = nil, labels: MonarchSecretFieldLabels = MonarchSecretFieldLabels(), onCopy: (@MainActor (String) -> Void)? = nil)

struct MonarchSecretFieldLabels { init(show: (@Sendable (String) -> String)? = nil, copy: (@Sendable (String) -> String)? = nil, copied: String? = nil, copiedAnnouncement: String? = nil, setPrompt: String? = nil, setDescription: String? = nil, hidden: String? = nil, error: (@Sendable (String) -> String)? = nil) }

options.name: label
options.description: What the secret is, such as "API key". Shown above the field and used in the names of the reveal and copy buttons.

options.name: text
options.description: The secret. Bind a constant for a read-only secret.

options.name: prompt
options.description: Placeholder shown while the field is empty.

options.name: helper
options.description: Supporting text under the field.

options.name: error
options.description: Error message; replaces the helper while present.

options.name: isSet
options.description: A value is saved on the server but not sent to the device. The empty field shows "Saved. Enter a new value to replace it" and the hint says a value is saved. Leaving it empty keeps the saved value; the app decides what to send.

options.name: isRevealable
options.description: Shows the reveal toggle.

options.name: isCopyable
options.description: Shows a copy button. It copies the current text while it stays masked.

options.name: isReadOnly
options.description: Shows the secret as read-only text (masked with one dot per character until revealed) instead of an editable field.

options.name: isRevealed
options.description: Whether the secret is shown as text. Without it the component keeps the state itself, starting masked.

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for the built-in strings: show, copy, copied, copiedAnnouncement, setPrompt, setDescription, hidden and error.

options.name: onCopy
options.description: Runs with the copied text after each copy.

states.name: masked
states.description: Default. A SecureField; the toggle shows an eye symbol and its value is off.

states.name: revealed
states.description: A TextField with the secret as text; the toggle shows a crossed eye and its value is on.

states.name: set, not shown
states.description: Empty with the "saved" placeholder and hint. Reveal and copy are disabled until the user types a replacement.

states.name: empty
states.description: Reveal and copy are disabled and drawn in the disabled text colour.

states.name: copied
states.description: For two seconds after a copy the copy symbol becomes a checkmark and the button is named "Copied".

states.name: read-only
states.description: The secret is text on the subtle fill, one dot per character while masked, selectable while revealed.

states.name: focused
states.description: Draws the theme's focus ring around the field.

states.name: error
states.description: Danger border, and an icon and message under the field.

states.name: disabled
states.description: Subtle background, the disabled text colour and disabled buttons, set with disabled(_:).

appearance: The same field as MonarchTextField: a surface fill with an input border and medium corners, the secret in the monospaced code type role in the default text colour, and the reveal and copy symbols in the muted text colour at the trailing edge. The colours come from the theme roles, so light, dark and both high-contrast themes follow the theme.
platformNotes: The web has sm, md and lg sizes; iOS has one size, the size of MonarchTextField. The web asks browser password managers to ignore the field with autocomplete and vendor attributes; iOS has no public API that keeps the Passwords bar off a SecureField, so the system may still offer it. On iOS a copied secret is local only (not sent through Universal Clipboard); iOS has no pasteboard flag that hides an item from clipboard history. Read-only is an isReadOnly flag instead of the input's readonly attribute. Android has the same parameters.
accessibility: The field is one VoiceOver element: label, then the secure value, then a hint with the error (spoken as "Error: …"), the "saved" description when isSet and the field is empty, or the helper text.
The reveal control is given to VoiceOver as a standard Toggle named "Show <label>" in both states; its value says whether the secret is shown.
The copy button is named "Copy <label>", becomes "Copied" for two seconds, plays the success haptic and announces "Copied to clipboard".
A read-only secret is spoken as "Hidden" while masked and as its text only while revealed.
Reveal and copy are disabled while the field is empty, including a saved secret that is not shown.
A new error message is announced when it appears, and is shown with an icon and text, not colour alone.
The field and each button have a 44-point touch target, and the text scales with Dynamic Type.
edgeCases: An empty error string counts as no error.
Revealing swaps the SecureField for a TextField; focus moves to the new field when the old one had it.
The system may clear a SecureField when editing starts again after the secret was hidden.
A long read-only secret stays on one line and is shortened in the middle; copy still copies all of it.
Copy is available while the secret is masked; it never reveals it.
Autocorrection and capitalisation are off in both states.

appearance: A MonarchSectionCard: the title and description in the section header styles, rows with the device icon in the muted text colour, the label in the strong body style, a subtle success badge, caption lines in the muted text colour and ghost Sign out buttons. The footnote sits in the card's subtle footer bar. All colours are theme roles, so light, dark and both high-contrast themes follow.
platformNotes: The parity map names List rows; the rows are a VStack inside a MonarchSectionCard, like the web's SectionCard and MonarchDeviceList, because the list sits inside the app's own scrolling settings screen where a nested List would not size itself. The web's confirmation is a ConfirmDialog that stays open while the request runs; on iOS it is the system alert, which closes when a button is tapped, so the pending state moves to the button and a failure appears as a notice in the card. The web's per-row hint (a hover title with the full user agent) has no touch equivalent and is left out, as is its describeUserAgent helper: an iOS app gets the session label from its server. The web's headingLevel has no iOS equivalent (the title is a header) and its locale prop is the SwiftUI locale environment. Android builds the same component, also experimental. Several closures are optional (onRetry, onSignOut, onSignOutOthers). Pass each one with its label: Swift gives a single unlabelled trailing closure to the first parameter that accepts it, which is onRetry.
accessibility: The title has the header trait (from MonarchSectionCard).

Each session is one element whose label is the session's label and whose value is This device, the detail and the times, built by a tested pure function; the current session is a word, not only a colour.
The device icon is decorative and hidden.
Sign out is a separate MonarchButton with a 44-point touch target, named "Sign out <label>".
The confirmations are system alerts with a destructive button and a cancel button.
Each result and each failure is posted as an announcement.
Rows stack the button under the text when they do not fit, so nothing is cut off at the largest text sizes.
edgeCases: The current session can be signed out too; its confirmation says the person will need to sign in again on this device.
Sign out other devices is hidden when the current session is the only one.
The app removes signed-out sessions from sessions after the handler returns; the list does not remove them itself.
Only one sign-out runs at a time.

title: SettingsPage
wrapsNative: NavigationStack(path:) with a List of NavigationLink(value:) rows and navigationDestination(for:) that opens each section as a Form screen, a toolbar Save (ToolbarItem(placement: .confirmationAction)), monarchUnsavedChangesGuard on the back button, and confirmationDialog for the danger zone; NavigationSplitView with List(selection:) on iPad
summary: A recipe, not a component: a settings screen as a list of sections, each opening its own screen with its settings, Save in the toolbar, a guard before leaving unsaved changes, and the danger zone last.
whenToUse: An app or workspace has several groups of settings (profile, notifications, members) that people change from time to time.
whenNotToUse: For one short group of settings, use the settings-section recipe: one Form with Save and Discard in the toolbar. For settings that apply as soon as they change, leave out Save and the guard.
api: NavigationStack(path: $path) { List { Section { NavigationLink(value: pane) { Label { title; summary } icon: { Image(systemName:) } } }; Section { NavigationLink(value: .danger) { … } } }.navigationTitle(_:).navigationDestination(for: Pane.self) { pane in … } }

Form { Section { Toggle(_:isOn:); Picker(_:selection:content:) } footer: { … } }.navigationTitle(_:).toolbar { ToolbarItem(placement: .confirmationAction) { Button("Save") { … }.disabled(!isDirty) } }
.monarchUnsavedChangesGuard(isPresented:hasChanges:onSave:onLeave:)
.confirmationDialog(_:isPresented:titleVisibility:actions:message:) for the danger zone
NavigationSplitView(sidebar: { List(selection:) { … } }, detail: { … }) with a selection binding that asks before changing section

options.name: panes
options.type: A Hashable enum of the app's sections
options.description: One case per group of settings, with a title, a one-line summary of the current value and a symbol; the danger zone is the last case, in its own list section.

options.name: path
options.description: The navigation path; empty shows the list. The guard's onLeave removes the last screen.

options.name: draft and saved
options.description: The section edits a draft; Save copies it to the saved value. isDirty is draft != saved and drives Save and the guard.

options.name: onSave
options.description: Saves the open section, from the toolbar Save and from Save and leave in the guard. A thrown error keeps the person on the screen.

states.name: list
states.description: The title and one row per section, each with a symbol, its title and a summary, and a disclosure chevron from NavigationLink.

states.name: detail
states.description: The section's settings in a Form with Save in the toolbar; Save is disabled until something changes.

states.name: unsaved changes
states.description: Save is enabled; the back button is replaced by MonarchUnsavedChangesGuard's, which asks to save, discard or keep editing; the back swipe is off.

states.name: danger zone
states.description: The last row, in the strong danger colour with a warning symbol, opens the danger-zone recipe: a destructive button that asks in a confirmation dialog.

states.name: iPad
states.description: NavigationSplitView shows the list and the open section side by side; changing section with unsaved changes asks first through the guarded selection binding. It collapses to the stack on iPhone.

appearance: System grouped list and Form in every theme, with Monarch text styles, the summary in the muted text colour, controls tinted with the accent colour and the danger row in the strong danger colour. The navigation bar, toolbar and confirmation dialogs are the system ones.
platformNotes: The web ships SettingsPage: a title, a section navigation (a sticky side list, a scrolling strip on phones), all sections on one long page, a page-wide save bar and a guard on leaving. iOS follows the system Settings pattern instead, like Android: the screen is a list of sections, each opens its own screen and saves on its own, and the back button returns to the list. The web's save bar becomes Save in the toolbar (the form-actions-bar entry); Discard is offered by the guard on leaving. On iPad NavigationSplitView (the split-layout entry) replaces the web's side navigation. The web's interceptLinks, guardRef and activeSection have no iOS equivalent: the guard covers the back button and the sheet swipe, and the app owns the navigation path. Android ships the same recipe with ListItem rows, BackHandler, MonarchSectionCard, MonarchFormActionsBar and MonarchUnsavedChangesGuard.
accessibility: Each section row is a NavigationLink, one VoiceOver element with the button trait, its title and summary read together.
The danger zone is named by its title and a warning symbol, not by colour alone.
Save is a toolbar button that is read as dimmed while there is nothing to save.
While there are unsaved changes the guard's back button asks with a system confirmation dialog; the destructive choice has the destructive role, and the escape gesture keeps editing.
Deleting the workspace asks in a system confirmation dialog whose title and message VoiceOver reads.
edgeCases: Keep each row's summary to the current value; long summaries wrap at large text sizes.
Save per section: a change in one section never waits for another.
When the save throws, the guard shows the error in an alert and the person stays on the screen.
On iPad, a sidebar change while the guard is asking is kept as the pending section and opened after Save and leave or Discard.

title: SettingsSection
wrapsNative: Form with Section(content:header:footer:), Toggle, Picker and Button(role: .destructive) rows, toolbar with ToolbarItem(placement: .cancellationAction) and .confirmationAction for Discard and Save, confirmationDialog, and redacted(reason: .placeholder) for loading; MonarchSectionCard for a card on a scrolling page
summary: A recipe, not a component: a titled group of settings as a Form section with a header and a footer, Save and Discard in the toolbar while there are unsaved changes, a danger zone section, and a loading state through redacted.
whenToUse: For a settings screen of grouped options, the way iOS Settings and every system app lay them out. Use the MonarchSectionCard form when settings sit on a scrolling page among other cards, for example on iPad.
whenNotToUse: For a single toggle inside other content, use a Toggle row on its own. For a long form people fill in once, use a Form with MonarchFormField rows and a submit button.
api: Form { Section { Toggle(_:isOn:); Picker(_:selection:content:) } header: { Text(title) } footer: { Text(description) } }
Section { Button(_:role: .destructive, action:) } header: { Text("Danger zone") }
.toolbar { ToolbarItem(placement: .cancellationAction) { Button("Discard") }; ToolbarItem(placement: .confirmationAction) { Button("Save") } }
.redacted(reason: isLoading ? .placeholder : [])
MonarchSectionCard(_:description:content:actions:footer:) with MonarchButton("Save changes", variant: .primary) in the footer

options.name: isDirty
options.description: The draft differs from the saved settings: Discard and Save are enabled.

options.name: isLoading
options.description: The settings are loading: the form is redacted and disabled.

options.name: danger zone
options.description: Destructive actions in their own section, each behind a confirmationDialog.

options.name: no access
options.description: When the person cannot change the settings, disable the controls and say who can in the section footer, or show MonarchEmptyState in place of the form.

states.name: ready
states.description: The sections with their headers, rows and footers; Save and Discard are disabled while nothing has changed.

states.name: dirty
states.description: Save and Discard are enabled in the toolbar; in the card form, "You have unsaved changes." and the two buttons appear in the footer.

states.name: loading
states.description: redacted(reason: .placeholder) draws the rows as placeholders and disabled stops input.

states.name: danger zone
states.description: A section whose button has the destructive role and opens a confirmation.

states.name: no access
states.description: Disabled rows with a footer that says who can change them.

appearance: The system grouped form: section headers and footers in the system's secondary styles, rows on the grouped background, switches and pickers tinted with the accent fill, destructive buttons in the system red. The card form uses the MonarchSectionCard surface and Monarch buttons. Both follow the dark and high-contrast appearances.
platformNotes: The parity map named a MonarchSettingsSectionStyle for Form sections (Android planned a MonarchSettingsSection type and shipped a recipe). Following the native-first rule this is a recipe on iOS as well: SwiftUI has no SectionStyle to customise, and a Form Section already gives the titled group, header, footer, grouped rows, Dynamic Type and VoiceOver order that iOS settings use, so a Monarch style or type would only imitate it. The web's save footer becomes Save and Discard in the toolbar, the iOS pattern for editing screens; the web's sticky footer is not needed because the toolbar stays visible. The web's SettingsRow is a Form row (Toggle, Picker, LabeledContent) and its SettingsActionRow is a Button row. The web's loading skeleton is redacted(reason: .placeholder), and its no-access notice is a footer or MonarchEmptyState. On a scrolling page the web's card look is MonarchSectionCard with the buttons in its footer.
accessibility: Section headers are read as headings by VoiceOver in a Form, and footers are read after their rows.
Toggles and pickers are the system controls, with their roles, values and labels.
Save and Discard are toolbar buttons with text labels and are read as dimmed while disabled.
Destructive actions use the destructive role and confirm before acting.
While loading, the redacted rows are disabled, so nothing can be changed by accident.
edgeCases: Long titles and footers wrap in the Form.
Leaving the screen with unsaved changes should ask first: pair it with the unsaved-changes-guard recipe.
Settings that apply at once (a single switch) need no Save: drop the toolbar buttons.

platformNotes: The web ShareDialog is a component with a trigger, a dialog, a combobox with email invites, a native select for roles, a members list, a general access select, a main link with copy and a list of share links with passwords, expiry, views and revoke. MonarchEntityPicker, the Pickers and MonarchCopyField are named by their labels; the role and access menus are standard pickers read with their value.
Each MonarchMemberRow reads the name, email, role and status, with its role menu and Remove as separate controls.

Keep the owner's role locked (canChangeRole: false) and the signed-in person with isSelf: true.

title: Sheet
wrapsNative: sheet(isPresented:onDismiss:content:) with presentationDetents, presentationDragIndicator and interactiveDismissDisabled; inspector(isPresented:content:) for a panel at the side
summary: A modal panel attached to an edge of the screen is the system sheet, which rises from the bottom, with detents for its height. A panel at the side is the inspector. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: For a task that is finished or cancelled before going back: a longer form, filters, a picker, details of a record on a phone. Use detents to keep part of the screen behind it in view.
whenNotToUse: Not for a short question (use alert or confirmationDialog), not for content that must cover the whole screen (use fullScreenCover), and not for a preview beside a list at regular width (use inspector).
api: func sheet<Content: View>(isPresented: Binding<Bool>, onDismiss: (() -> Void)? = nil, content: @escaping () -> Content) -> some View
func sheet<Item: Identifiable, Content: View>(item: Binding<Item?>, onDismiss: (() -> Void)? = nil, content: @escaping (Item) -> Content) -> some View

func presentationDragIndicator(_ visibility: Visibility) -> some View
func interactiveDismissDisabled(_ isDisabled: Bool = true) -> some View
func presentationBackground<S: ShapeStyle>(_ style: S) -> some View

states.description: The sheet covers the lower part of the screen or all of it, by detent. The content behind is dimmed and not interactive.

states.name: resting at a detent
states.description: With several detents the person drags the sheet between heights; a detent selection binding reports the current one.

states.name: dismissal blocked
states.description: interactiveDismissDisabled(true) stops the swipe down, for unsaved changes or while saving.

appearance: The system draws the sheet, its corner radius, the grabber and the dimming in every theme. presentationBackground with a theme colour sets the fill; the content uses Monarch components.
platformNotes: The web Sheet attaches to any edge (right by default) and has sizes sm to full, a header, body and footer, a close button, a drag handle and a busy state. An iOS sheet always rises from the bottom; the web's sizes are detents (.medium, .large, .height, .fraction), handle is presentationDragIndicator, busy and escapeGuard are interactiveDismissDisabled, and closeOnOutsideClick is the system's swipe and tap behaviour. The header, body and footer are ordinary content: a NavigationStack with a title and toolbar buttons, or a VStack. A side panel (the web's start and end sides) is the inspector, which is a column at regular width; there is no top sheet. Android uses ModalBottomSheet in the same way.
accessibility: System behaviour: the sheet confines VoiceOver, Switch Control and keyboard focus until it is dismissed, and returns focus to the presenting screen.
System behaviour: the escape gesture and a swipe down dismiss it unless interactiveDismissDisabled is set.
Keep a visible button that closes the sheet (Done or Cancel); the swipe is not available to everyone.
Mark the title of the sheet as a header so VoiceOver users can find the start of it.
edgeCases: At compact height (a phone in landscape) the system presents the sheet at full height.
On iPad at regular width the system presents a sheet as a centred card.
A sheet presented from inside another sheet stacks; avoid more than two levels.
presentationBackgroundInteraction(.enabled(upThrough:)) lets the content behind a low detent be used, which makes the sheet non-modal up to that height.

appearance: Rows are separated by the subtle divider; names are in the default text colour and descriptions, hours and counts in the muted colour. A shift cell keeps the event chip's colours (the shift colour only as the bar and a light tint), a day off uses the muted background, and an unassigned day a dashed default border. Today uses the strong accent and an info badge. The grid's header and footer rows sit on the subtle background. High contrast themes use their own roles; every state is also written.
platformNotes: The web ShiftRoster is always a table of people by days with a roving-focus keyboard grid and Delete to clear. On a phone that table does not fit, so iOS shows one day at a time with a MonarchTabs strip (or one person at a time) and keeps the table for an iPad or a wide window (automatic picks it through ViewThatFits when every column fits). Each cell is a system Menu with an inline Picker, so the current choice is checked and VoiceOver, the keyboard and pointer work as in any iOS menu; the web's arrow-key grid navigation is not reproduced. The web takes ISO dates, a BCP 47 locale and an hour cycle; iOS takes Date values matched in a Calendar, the environment's locale and uses24HourClock. Android names the same types and options (members, shifts, from, value, days, layout, readOnly, loading, showTotals, today, is24Hour, error, onMemberClick, labels, empty); iOS follows SwiftUI conventions: the value is a Binding with onChange reporting each MonarchShiftRosterChange, the flags are isReadOnly, isLoading, showsTotals and uses24HourClock, onMemberClick is onSelectMember, and enabled is the environment's .disabled(_:). The plan's drag to assign is not offered on any platform: the web has no drag either, and a menu per cell is the touch and VoiceOver pattern. Day tabs show one line ("Wed 4" or "Today") because MonarchTabs labels are one line; Android shows the weekday above the date. Experimental because it is a product pattern not yet adopted by a Rook iOS app. Several closures are optional (onChange, onSelectMember). Pass each one with its label: Swift gives a single unlabelled trailing closure to the first parameter that accepts it, which is onChange.
accessibility: Each editable cell is a system Menu, one element with a touch target of at least 44 points, named "<person>, <day>: <assignment>", for example "Alex Kim, Tuesday, November 3, Today: Night, N, 22:00 to 06:00, overnight"; the short name is added only in the grid, where it is what is shown.
The cell's menu is headed by the person and the day; the current choice is checked by the system Picker, and each shift is read with its spoken time range.
Read-only cells are one element with the same name and no action; with .disabled(true) cells are read as dimmed.
Day and person tabs are a MonarchTabs strip named "Day" or "Person"; the selected tab has the selected trait.
The day's date under the tabs is a header read with "Today" for today; after an assignment the new number working is announced.
Each person is one element read as "name, description, Hours: total"; with onSelectMember it is a button with a 44-point target.

The grid is a container named "Shift roster"; day headers are headers read as the full date, the hours column is read as "Hours: 40 h" and footer counts with the date, "Wednesday, November 4: 3 working".
Avatars are decorative; no state is shown by colour alone.
At the accessibility text sizes the cell moves under the person or day so no text is cut, and the automatic layout never shows the grid above xxLarge; grid columns scale with Dynamic Type.
edgeCases: Keys in value may be any time on the day; they are matched in calendar, and a change replaces any key on that day with the start of the day.
An assignment to a shift id that is not among shifts reads as not assigned and counts no hours.
A shift whose end equals its start lasts 24 hours and is overnight.
days is clamped to 1 to 62.
Choosing the current assignment again changes nothing and calls no onChange.
Hours are rounded to one decimal in the locale's number format.
Shift times are formatted on a fixed UTC day, so a daylight-saving change in calendar does not move them.
The roster does not scroll vertically; put it in a scrolling screen. The grid scrolls sideways when forced with layout: .grid.
Long names and descriptions wrap; nothing is truncated.

On iOS it is a recipe, because the request, the session and navigation belong to the app. Autofill comes from the content types: .username on the email field and the .password content type that MonarchPasswordInput's current purpose sets, together with the app's associated domain (webcredentials), so iOS offers saved passwords and passkeys. Passkey sign-in is the system sheet from ASAuthorizationController with an ASAuthorizationPlatformPublicKeyCredentialProvider assertion request; for passkeys in the keyboard's suggestions, call performAutoFillAssistedRequests() when the screen appears. On a device add keyboardType(.emailAddress), textInputAutocapitalization(.never) and autocorrectionDisabled() to the email field; they are left out of the compiled example because the host build also targets macOS. The web's identifier modes (username, email or username) are the field's label and content type. Android composes the same recipe with Credential Manager.

The system passkey sheet is the system's.

Trim spaces around the email but never change the password.

whenToUse: While content loads and its layout is known: build the view with sample data and redact it, so the placeholder has the size of the real content.
whenNotToUse: For a wait with no known layout, use a ProgressView. For a failure, use MonarchErrorState or MonarchInlineErrorRetry.

states.description: Text and images are replaced by rounded placeholder shapes in the foreground colour.

states.name: loaded
states.description: Pass an empty reason set to show the content.

appearance: System placeholder shapes, which take the foreground colour of the redacted views, so they follow the theme's text colours in every theme. They do not animate.
platformNotes: The parity map lists a shimmer modifier beside the redaction. No shimmer is shipped: a modifier would be a Swift type, which a native-adoption entry does not have, and the system placeholder is static, so there is nothing to stop under Reduce Motion. Android builds MonarchSkeleton and the web Skeleton shimmers; if the same is wanted here it is a separate build entry. The web shape, width and height props have no equivalent, because the placeholder takes the shape of the real views.
accessibility: System behaviour: redacted text is still read by VoiceOver as its sample content. Group the redacted region as one element with accessibilityElement(children: .ignore) and give it a label such as "Loading contact".
The placeholder does not move, so Reduce Motion needs no handling.
edgeCases: Monarch components draw their text and icons with Text and Image, so they redact with the rest of the layout.
Backgrounds, borders and custom shapes are not redacted.
unredacted() keeps one part readable while the rest loads.

name: MonarchSlaIndicator
title: SlaIndicator
wrapsNative: TimelineView with a custom TimelineSchedule, Text, Duration.UnitsFormatStyle, Date.FormatStyle
summary: A service-level target at a glance: on track, at risk, breached, paused, met or not applicable, with the time left or overdue, as a chip or as an icon with text.
whenToUse: In ticket and task lists and headers (chip), and in the rows of a detail panel that lists the targets of one item (text).
whenNotToUse: Not for a general status; use MonarchBadge. Not for a plain date or age; use the platform's relative date formatting (see RelativeTime).
api: init(_ state: MonarchSlaIndicatorState, dueAt: Date? = nil, warnBefore: TimeInterval? = nil, target: String? = nil, variant: MonarchSlaIndicatorVariant = .chip, hasEarlierBreach: Bool = false, showsNotApplicable: Bool = false, isLive: Bool = true, announcesChanges: Bool = false, now: Date? = nil, labels: MonarchSlaIndicatorLabels = MonarchSlaIndicatorLabels(), onStateChange: (@MainActor (MonarchSlaIndicatorState) -> Void)? = nil)
enum MonarchSlaIndicatorState { case onTrack, atRisk, breached, paused, met, notApplicable }
enum MonarchSlaIndicatorVariant { case chip, text }

struct MonarchSlaIndicatorLabels { init(onTrack: String? = nil, atRisk: String? = nil, breached: String? = nil, paused: String? = nil, met: String? = nil, notApplicable: String? = nil, notApplicableMark: String? = nil, remaining: (@Sendable (String) -> String)? = nil, overdue: (@Sendable (String) -> String)? = nil, duration: (@Sendable (TimeInterval) -> String)? = nil, due: (@Sendable (String) -> String)? = nil, earlierBreach: String? = nil, changed: (@Sendable (String, String?) -> String)? = nil) }

options.name: state
options.description: The state the server reported: onTrack, atRisk, breached, paused, met or notApplicable. A running state is re-derived from dueAt and the clock.

options.name: dueAt
options.description: When the target is due. It drives the countdown ("2h 15m left") and the overdue time ("Overdue 40m").

options.name: warnBefore
options.description: Turns an on-track target at risk once it is due within this many seconds. By default the state is trusted.

options.name: target
options.description: The name of the target, such as "First response". Read by VoiceOver, not shown.

options.name: variant
options.description: chip is a compact rounded rectangle; text is an icon and text without a surface.

options.name: hasEarlierBreach
options.description: An earlier target of the same item was breached. VoiceOver says so.

options.name: showsNotApplicable
options.description: Write a missing target as "No SLA" and not as a dash.

options.name: isLive
options.description: Whether a running target with a due time follows the clock by itself.

options.name: announcesChanges
options.description: Announce a change of state to VoiceOver. For one prominent indicator, not for every row of a list.

options.name: now
options.description: A fixed reference time, which also stops the clock.

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for the built-in strings, including the duration formatter.

options.name: onStateChange
options.description: Called when the shown state changes after the indicator appeared, such as when a countdown runs out.

states.name: onTrack
states.description: Clock icon, muted text, no fill. Shows the time left when dueAt is given.

states.name: atRisk
states.description: Clock icon, warning colours; the chip has a tinted fill and a border. Shows the time left.

states.name: breached
states.description: Exclamation icon. The chip is solid danger; the text variant is danger-coloured text. Shows the time overdue when dueAt has passed.

states.name: paused
states.description: Pause icon, muted text; the chip has a muted fill. No countdown.

states.name: met
states.description: Checkmark icon, success-coloured text, no fill.

states.name: notApplicable
states.description: No icon, subtle text in the regular weight: a dash, or "No SLA" with showsNotApplicable.

appearance: Caption text with a small icon. Colours come from the theme by role: muted text for on track and paused, the warning roles for at risk, solid danger for a breached chip, the strong success colour for met and the subtle text colour when no target applies. In the high-contrast themes a chip that has no border of its own gets the strong border colour.
platformNotes: The parity map named MonarchBadge with Text(timerInterval:). Neither fits: the badge has no border on a tinted fill, no transparent form and a capsule shape, and Text(timerInterval:) writes a running clock (1:59:07), not "2h 15m left", and cannot change the state at the due time. The indicator draws its own chip and uses TimelineView with a schedule aligned to the due time, so it redraws once a minute and exactly when it becomes at risk or breached. The web state none is notApplicable here, because none reads as Optional.none in Swift. The web shows the due date in a tooltip; iOS reads it as the accessibility value. The web live interval and locale options are not offered: redraws are aligned to the minute and the locale comes from the environment. The web file also exports SlaTargetList; on iOS that is LabeledContent rows with the text variant (see the last example). Android has the same component.
accessibility: One accessibility element. The label is the target name and the time left or overdue in words ("First response, 2 hours, 15 minutes left"), or the state name when there is no countdown.
The value is the state name when the label is a countdown, then the due date and time, then a note when an earlier target was breached.
Every state has its own icon and text, so the state does not depend on colour.
With announcesChanges a change of the shown state is posted as an announcement, such as "First response: Breached".
The text scales with Dynamic Type and wraps; the icon scales with it.
The indicator is not interactive.
edgeCases: A running target whose due time has passed is shown as breached even if the server still reports on track.

Durations are whole minutes rounded down, in at most two units: "<1m", "45m", "2h 15m", "3d 4h". Units are written by Duration.UnitsFormatStyle in the locale of the environment; only "<1m" comes from the strings table.
A breached target without a due time, or with one in the future, shows "Breached".
paused, met, breached and notApplicable are never changed by the clock, and their indicators are not redrawn by time.
With now set, or isLive false, the text is computed once per draw and does not advance.
onStateChange and the announcement fire for a change of the shown state, whether the clock or a new state value caused it.

whenToUse: In a notes, document or message composer where people insert headings, lists and other blocks by typing a slash at the start of a line.
whenNotToUse: For @mentions, use MonarchMentionPicker. For a fixed set of formatting actions, use MonarchEditorToolbar.

options.name: query
options.description: The command being typed, from MonarchSlashMenuQuery.find. Nothing is drawn while it is nil.

options.name: items
options.description: Every item the menu offers. The menu filters them by the query with MonarchSlashMenu.filter.

options.name: groupOrder
options.description: Group headings in display order. Groups not listed follow in the order they first appear.

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for the list's spoken name, the empty text and the count announcement.

options.name: onSelect
options.description: Receives the chosen item. Replace the query with query.replacing(in:with:) and set the query to nil.

states.name: closed
states.description: No query: nothing is drawn.

states.name: results
states.description: The matching items under their group headings; more than four rows scroll.

states.name: disabled item
states.description: Icon and text in the disabled colour; the row cannot be chosen.

states.name: nothing matches
states.description: One line, "Nothing matches “/xyz”", in the muted text colour.

appearance: A strip on the surface colour with a subtle top border. Group headings are captions in the muted text colour; each row has a muted icon, the label in the default text colour and the description in the muted text colour. Disabled rows use the disabled text colour. The roles follow light, dark and high-contrast themes.
platformNotes: The web SlashMenu is a popover beside the caret, with the highlight moved by arrow keys while focus stays in the field (aria-activedescendant), and hooks that wire it to a textarea or a rich-text editor. iOS gives no caret rectangle to a SwiftUI text field, so the menu is a full-width strip above the keyboard, the same placement as MonarchMentionPicker, and a row is chosen by tapping it; there is no highlighted row and no arrow-key handling. The web hooks become MonarchSlashMenuQuery.find and replacing; the web's filterSlashMenuItems is MonarchSlashMenu.filter with the same ranking. The menu filters the items itself, where the web takes them already filtered. Android shares this design.
accessibility: Each item is a button named by its label and description, for example "Heading, Large section title"; disabled items are dimmed and not activatable.
The list is a container named "Insert block"; group headings have the header trait.
The number of options, or "Nothing matches “/xyz”", is announced as the list changes, so focus can stay in the text field.
Rows are at least 44 points high and grow with Dynamic Type; icons are decorative.
edgeCases: A slash inside a line (1/2, a path) never opens the menu with the default line-start position; use .wordStart to allow it after a space.
A space, punctuation or more than 24 characters after the slash closes the menu, so typing on continues normally.
Keep the strip in the same safe-area inset as the composer so it stays above the keyboard.

title: SortableGrid
wrapsNative: LazyVGrid with draggable(_:) and dropDestination(for:action:isTargeted:) on each tile, MonarchDragHandle with accessibility actions, AccessibilityNotification.Announcement
summary: Tiles that people reorder in two dimensions by dragging, or one place or one row at a time with accessibility actions, with each move announced.
whenToUse: For a dashboard of widgets, a photo or card board, or any grid whose order the person arranges.
whenNotToUse: For a single column of rows, use a List with onMove(perform:) (see reorderable-list). For moving items between groups, use a Kanban board.
api: init(_ items: Binding<[Item]>, itemLabel: KeyPath<Item, String>, columns: Int? = nil, minimumItemWidth: CGFloat? = nil, isItemDisabled: ((Item) -> Bool)? = nil, labels: MonarchSortableGridLabels = MonarchSortableGridLabels(), onReorder: (@MainActor (_ from: Int, _ to: Int) -> Void)? = nil, @ViewBuilder content: @escaping (Item, MonarchSortableGridItemState) -> Content)
struct MonarchSortableGridItemState { let index: Int; let isDropTarget: Bool; let isDisabled: Bool }
struct MonarchSortableGridLabels { var handle: (@Sendable (String) -> String)?; var moved, dropped: (@Sendable (String, Int, Int) -> String)?; var actions: [MonarchDragHandleDirection: String] }

options.name: items
options.description: The items in order. Item is Identifiable. The grid writes the new order after each move.

options.name: itemLabel
options.description: The plain-text name of an item, used in the handle's name and the announcements.

options.name: columns
options.description: A fixed number of columns. Without it, as many columns of minimumItemWidth as fit.

options.name: minimumItemWidth
options.description: The smallest tile width for adaptive columns, scaled with Dynamic Type.

options.name: isItemDisabled
options.description: Items that cannot be moved. Other items can still move past them.

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for the handle name, the two announcements and the move action names.

options.name: onReorder
options.description: Called after each finished move with the old and the new index, after items is updated.

options.name: content
options.description: Draws a tile. The state gives the index, whether a drag is over it and whether it is disabled.

states.name: drop target
states.description: While a dragged tile is over a tile, that tile has an accent outline and its state has isDropTarget.

states.name: disabled item
states.description: Not draggable; its handle is drawn in the disabled colour and has no actions.

states.name: disabled grid
states.description: With .disabled(true) no tile can be dragged or moved.

appearance: The grid draws only the handle in each tile's top trailing corner (muted grip, disabled colour when locked) and a strong-accent outline around the tile a drag is over. The tiles are the app's own views.
platformNotes: The web grid follows the pointer and slides the other tiles out of the way while dragging; on iOS the system drag shows a lifted preview and the order changes on drop. The web picks up a tile with Space and moves it with the arrow keys; on iOS each handle offers named actions (Move up, Move down, Move backward, Move forward) to VoiceOver, Switch Control and Full Keyboard Access. The web's uncontrolled defaultItems is not offered: the order is always a binding. The default minimum tile width is 160 points instead of the web's 12rem, so a phone shows two columns.
accessibility: Each tile has a drag handle named Reorder and the item's name, with move actions for each direction that the column count allows (up and down only in one column).
After a move with an action the new position is announced: "Design review moved to position 3 of 8."; after a drop: "Design review dropped at position 3 of 8."
Backward and forward follow reading order, so they are mirrored in right-to-left layouts with the grid.
The drop target is shown by an outline, not by colour alone.
The handle keeps a 44 by 44 point touch target; adaptive columns become fewer and wider at larger text sizes.
edgeCases: Drops of text from another grid or another app are ignored: the payload carries the grid's own id.
An action that would move a tile past the first or last place, or above the first row, does nothing.
An empty items array draws nothing.
Tiles in the same row take the height the grid gives them; give tiles a minimum height when they should line up.

name: MonarchSpaceSwitcher
title: SpaceSwitcher
wrapsNative: Button with MonarchButtonStyle (.ghost) presenting .sheet with NavigationStack, List, .searchable(text:prompt:), Link and presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
summary: Chooses which Space of the workspace the app shows, "All spaces" or one Space, from a button that opens a sheet with a searchable list, New Space and Manage Spaces.
whenToUse: In an app that scopes its content by Space: in the navigation bar, a sidebar header or a screen header, wherever the current Space is chosen.
whenNotToUse: To switch workspace use MonarchWorkspaceSwitcher. To filter one list by team or department use a filter in the list's own toolbar, such as a menu Picker.
api: init(selection: Binding<String?>, spaces: [MonarchSpaceOption], size: MonarchButtonSize = .md, allowsAll: Bool = true, isLoading: Bool = false, isIconOnly: Bool = false, hidesWhenEmpty: Bool = true, manageURL: URL? = nil, labels: MonarchSpaceSwitcherLabels = MonarchSpaceSwitcherLabels(), onCreate: (@MainActor () -> Void)? = nil)
struct MonarchSpaceOption { init(id: String, name: String, description: String? = nil, systemImage: String? = nil) }
struct MonarchSpaceSwitcherLabels { init(label:, all:, placeholder:, search:, empty:, loading:, create:, manage:, cancel:) }

options.name: selection
options.description: The chosen Space id, nil for All spaces.

options.name: spaces
options.description: The Spaces this person can open, in display order.

options.name: size
options.description: The height and padding of the button.

options.name: allowsAll
options.description: Offers All spaces first. Without it a Space must stay chosen and the button reads Choose a Space until one is.

options.name: isLoading
options.description: The Spaces are still loading; the list shows a progress indicator with Loading spaces.

options.name: isIconOnly
options.description: Shows only the Space's symbol and the chevron, for a narrow bar. The name stays the spoken value.

options.name: hidesWhenEmpty
options.description: Shows nothing when there are no Spaces and nothing is loading.

options.name: manageURL
options.description: Adds Manage Spaces, a Link that opens this URL.

options.name: labels
options.description: Replacements for every built-in string.

options.name: onCreate
options.description: Adds New Space, which closes the sheet and runs this.

states.name: all spaces
states.description: Nothing chosen: the button shows the layers symbol and All spaces; All spaces is checked in the list.

states.name: one space
states.description: The button shows the Space's symbol and name; its row is checked and has the selected trait.

states.name: no choice
states.description: With allowsAll false and nothing chosen the button reads Choose a Space.

states.name: searching
states.description: The list keeps the Spaces whose name or description contains the text; All spaces is hidden; with no match it reads No spaces match.

states.name: loading
states.description: The list ends with a progress indicator and Loading spaces.

states.name: empty
states.description: With no Spaces and nothing loading nothing is shown, unless hidesWhenEmpty is false.

states.name: disabled
states.description: Through disabled(_:), the ghost button style's disabled colours; the sheet cannot open.

appearance: A ghost MonarchButtonStyle button: the Space's symbol, the name in the default text colour and an up-down chevron in the muted text colour. The sheet is a system inset List; rows have a muted symbol, the name, a caption description in the muted text colour and an accent check mark; the actions are accent-tinted. All colours are theme roles, so light, dark and both high-contrast themes follow.
platformNotes: The parity map lists combobox as a dependency; MonarchCombobox is a labelled form field, so the switcher uses its own button and the same system sheet, List and search field that the combobox uses. The web opens a popover with a listbox (arrow keys, Home and End, type to search) from EntityPicker; on iPhone the same choice is a sheet with a system List and the system search field, as the plan names, and keyboard navigation is the system's. The web's tooltip on the collapsed trigger is the spoken value here, since a phone has no hover. Manage Spaces opens the URL with the environment's openURL, which leaves the app, so the web's "opens in a new tab" text and manageExternal have no counterpart; createHref is onCreate. The web's controlled open state and align are not offered. A Space id that is no longer in the list reads as All spaces, as on the web. Android builds the same component.
accessibility: The button is one element named "Space" whose value is the current Space or All spaces, also when only the icon shows.
Each row is a button named by the Space and its description ("Engineering, 18 members"), built by a tested pure function.
The chosen row has the selected trait and a check mark, so the choice does not depend on colour.
Symbols are decorative and hidden.
Rows, New Space and Manage Spaces keep a 44-point touch target.
Search is the system search field; Cancel closes the sheet without a change.
edgeCases: A selected id that is not in spaces reads as All spaces (or Choose a Space when All spaces is not offered).
Choosing All spaces when allowsAll is false does nothing.
Long Space names stay on one line on the button and wrap in the list.
The switcher never stores the choice; the app keeps selection.

parityExceptions.reason: The web opens the list as a popover under the trigger, so the trigger and the list show together. On iPhone the same choice is a medium or large sheet over the screen, with the system search field and Cancel; the trigger sits behind the sheet. name: MonarchSparkline
title: Sparkline
wrapsNative: Shape (Path) with stroke and fill
summary: A word-sized trend line, area or bar chart for tables, stat cards and lists, with a text alternative.
whenToUse: Beside a number, to show where it has been: in a stat card, a table cell or a list row.
whenNotToUse: For a chart people read values from, with axes and a legend, use Swift Charts. Never as the only carrier of a value: show the number or a MonarchDeltaIndicator beside it.
api: MonarchSparkline.init(_ values: [Double?], label: String? = nil, summary: String? = nil, tone: MonarchTone? = nil, color: MonarchChartColor? = nil, variant: MonarchSparklineVariant = .line, range: ClosedRange<Double>? = nil, isInverted: Bool = false, showsLastPoint: Bool = true, notEnoughDataLabel: String? = nil, fullWidth: Bool = false, formatValue: ((Double) -> String)? = nil)

options.name: values
options.description: The values in order. nil, or a value that is not finite, is a gap.

options.name: label
options.description: The spoken name. Without it the sparkline is decorative and hidden.

options.name: summary
options.description: Replaces the spoken value "latest 9, low 3, high 9".

options.name: tone
options.description: A colour with meaning. nil takes the surrounding foreground style.

options.name: variant
options.description: line, area or bar.

options.name: range
options.description: Fixes the value range, so sparklines in a table share one scale.

options.name: isInverted
options.description: Draws smaller values higher, as for a rank.

options.name: showsLastPoint
options.description: Puts a dot on the latest point. Lines and areas only.

options.name: notEnoughDataLabel
options.description: Replaces the built-in text "Not enough data".

options.name: fullWidth
options.description: Fills the available width instead of 80 points.

options.name: formatValue
options.description: Writes the numbers of the spoken value. The default is a number in the current locale.

options.name: color
options.description: A chart series colour (a data slot of the theme); ignored when a tone is set.

states.name: line
states.description: A line that breaks at gaps, with a dot on the latest point and on every point that stands alone.

states.name: area
states.description: The line with a soft fill down to the baseline.

states.name: bar
states.description: One bar per value, from zero; negative values go down.

states.name: not enough data
states.description: Fewer than two values (one for bars): the text "Not enough data".

appearance: Without a tone the line takes the foreground style around it and the area a faint level of the same style. With a tone the line uses the tone's strong colour and the area its subtle colour, in every theme.
platformNotes: The web sizes are pixels; here the sparkline is 80 by 24 points and scales with Dynamic Type, or fills the width. The web tones current and accent, the series colours, the threshold option that picks a tone from the latest value, and markers on all points are not offered: pass the tone you want. The web domain is the range parameter. The chart runs from the leading edge, so it is mirrored in right-to-left layouts and the latest value is at the trailing end; the web one is not mirrored. Android uses the same names.
accessibility: With a label the sparkline is one element with the image trait: the label is its name and the value is "latest 11, low 3, high 11", followed by the name of the tone when it has one.
Without a label it is hidden from VoiceOver, so the numbers must be in text nearby.
The tone is spoken by name, so it does not depend on colour, and the numbers it stands for should be visible beside it.
The "Not enough data" text is read; with a label it becomes the value.
The sparkline scales with Dynamic Type. It does not animate.
edgeCases: A flat series is drawn in the middle of the height.
A value outside a fixed range is drawn at the edge.
Bars always include zero in their range; a zero value is a one-point bar.
A single value between two gaps is drawn as a dot, because a line cannot show it.

title: Spinner
wrapsNative: ProgressView() with .progressViewStyle(.circular)
summary: The standard spinner. Inside a Monarch theme it takes the accent colour from the tint. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: For a short wait of unknown length.
whenNotToUse: When the fraction is known, use the linear style.

name: MonarchButtonStyle
title: SplitButton
wrapsNative: Menu(content:label:primaryAction:) with .buttonStyle(.monarch(_:size:)); or an HStack of a Button and an icon-only Menu, both with .buttonStyle(.monarch(_:))
summary: A main action joined to a menu of alternatives, such as Save with Save as draft and Save and close: the standard Menu with a primary action and the Monarch button style.
whenToUse: When one action is the usual choice and a few related alternatives are needed now and then.
whenNotToUse: When no action is the default, use a menu button (Menu without primaryAction). When the alternatives are as common as the main action, show them as separate buttons.
api: Menu(content: () -> Content, label: () -> Label, primaryAction: () -> Void)
func buttonStyle(_ style: MonarchButtonStyle) -> some View  // .monarch(_ variant: MonarchButtonVariant = .secondary, size: MonarchButtonSize = .md, fullWidth: Bool = false)

options.name: variant
options.description: On .buttonStyle(.monarch(_:size:fullWidth:)): primary, secondary, ghost or danger. Use ghost for an icon-only trigger.

options.name: size
options.description: sm, md or lg. The touch target is at least 44 points at every size.

options.name: fullWidth
options.description: Whether the trigger fills the available width.

states.name: idle
states.description: One Monarch button. A tap runs the main action; a long press opens the alternatives.

states.name: pressed
states.description: The pressed colour of the variant.

states.name: disabled
states.description: disabled(true) disables the main action and the menu together. In the joined recipe, disable the arrow alone to keep the main action available.

appearance: The colours of the chosen Monarch button variant. The joined recipe draws two buttons of the same variant two points apart; the menu is the system's, in every theme.
platformNotes: The web SplitButton draws the main button and a separate arrow button with its own Tab stop and the name "More options for <label>". iOS's own idiom is Menu with primaryAction: one button, a tap for the main action and a long press for the alternatives, as in Mail and Safari. Because the long press is not visible, the second recipe joins a main button to a visible arrow Menu when the alternatives must be found by everyone. The web menuDisabled maps to disabling the arrow in that recipe. Android ships a MonarchSplitButton type.
accessibility: With primaryAction, VoiceOver activates the main action with a double tap and offers the menu in the actions rotor (system behaviour).
In the joined recipe the arrow is a separate element named "More options for <title>" by accessibilityLabel, and the pair is a container named after the main action.
The chevron is decorative.
Each button keeps a 44-point touch target.
edgeCases: A long press on a disabled Menu does nothing.
The long-press menu is not discoverable by sight; use the joined recipe when that matters.
On macOS (host builds only) Menu with primaryAction draws a split pull-down; iOS is the supported platform.
How VoiceOver announces the long-press menu was not checked on a device.

title: SplitInboxLayout
wrapsNative: NavigationSplitView(sidebar:detail:) with List(selection:) for the list and detail panes, and inspector(isPresented:content:) for the context pane; NavigationSplitView(sidebar:content:detail:) when the list has folders
summary: An inbox is the system's split view: the list and the detail are NavigationSplitView columns, and the context pane is an inspector. On iPhone one pane shows at a time with back navigation. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: For a list of items opened one at a time with extra context, such as a support inbox, mail or a queue of approvals.
whenNotToUse: For a list without a detail pane, use a List in a NavigationStack. For two panes only, see split-layout.
api: NavigationSplitView(columnVisibility:sidebar:detail:)
NavigationSplitView(sidebar:content:detail:)
List(_:id:selection:rowContent:)
.inspector(isPresented: Binding<Bool>, content:)
.inspectorColumnWidth(min:ideal:max:)

states.name: compact width
states.description: One pane at a time: the list, then the detail with a back button; the inspector is a sheet.

states.name: regular width
states.description: The list and the detail side by side; the inspector is a column at the trailing edge.

states.name: nothing selected
states.description: The detail shows an empty state.

states.name: context hidden
states.description: The toolbar button shows and hides the inspector.

appearance: System columns, separators and selection; the selection takes the accent through the tint. Rows, the empty state and the context content are Monarch components.
platformNotes: The parity map named a three-column NavigationSplitView. The web's three panes are list, detail and context; on iOS the context pane is an inspector, which the system shows as a trailing column on iPad and as a sheet on iPhone, while the three-column NavigationSplitView is for a folder sidebar before the list, shown in the second example. The web's breakpoints, pane toggles, resizing, focus management and list collapse are the system's: columnVisibility collapses the list, and inspectorColumnWidth sizes the context pane. Android uses the Material list-detail scaffold.
accessibility: System behaviour: the list is a list with selection, columns are separate containers for VoiceOver, and the back button returns to the list on iPhone.
The inspector toggle is a toolbar button whose label says what it does.
Selection is shown by the system highlight and the selected trait, not colour alone.
edgeCases: Keep the selection in state that survives size changes, so rotating an iPad does not lose the open item.
inspector needs iOS 17, the deployment target.
On iPhone the inspector is a sheet; give it presentationDetents if it is short.

title: SplitLayout
wrapsNative: NavigationSplitView(sidebar:detail:) with List(selection:) and navigationSplitViewColumnWidth(min:ideal:max:)
summary: The standard two-column NavigationSplitView: a list and the detail of the selected item side by side, and one pane at a time on a phone. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: For inbox-style screens: browsing a list while reading one item. Drive the detail from the list's selection.
whenNotToUse: For two panes that both stay on screen and are resized by the person use MonarchResizablePanels (see resizable-panels). For a single column of screens use NavigationStack.
api: NavigationSplitView(sidebar: () -> Sidebar, detail: () -> Detail)
NavigationSplitView(columnVisibility: Binding<NavigationSplitViewVisibility>, sidebar: () -> Sidebar, detail: () -> Detail)
func navigationSplitViewColumnWidth(min: CGFloat? = nil, ideal: CGFloat, max: CGFloat? = nil) -> some View
func navigationSplitViewStyle(_ style: some NavigationSplitViewStyle) -> some View

states.name: regular width
states.description: Both columns are shown. The selected row has the system's selection background.

states.name: compact width
states.description: One column is shown. Selecting a row pushes the detail, and the system back button returns to the list.

states.name: nothing selected
states.description: The detail column shows the placeholder the app supplies.

appearance: The system draws the columns, the divider between them and the navigation bars. Rows and the detail use Monarch text styles and theme colours; the selection highlight is the system's.
platformNotes: The web SplitLayout takes detailOpen, onBack and backLabel to show one pane below 768 pixels. NavigationSplitView does this itself: at a compact width it becomes a stack, and the back button and its label are the system's. The web's listWidth is navigationSplitViewColumnWidth, which proposes a width; the person cannot drag the column edge on iOS. listLabel and detailLabel are the navigation titles of the columns. Android uses the Material list-detail scaffold.
accessibility: System behaviour: each column is a navigation region with its title as a heading.
System behaviour: at a compact width the back button is named after the list's navigation title.
System behaviour: with a hardware keyboard the arrow keys move the selection in the list.
Give the detail a placeholder text when nothing is selected, so the empty column is not silent.
edgeCases: On a phone in portrait only one column is visible; the selection must be optional so the app can start on the list.
Clearing the selection at a compact width pops back to the list.
A NavigationSplitView inside a NavigationStack shows two navigation bars; make it the root of a scene or a presentation.

title: Stack
wrapsNative: VStack(alignment:spacing:content:) with spacing from theme.spacing
summary: The standard SwiftUI VStack with its spacing taken from the Monarch space scale. Monarch ships nothing.
whenToUse: For any column of views with even gaps. Pass theme.spacing.space2, space4 and so on as the spacing, never a number.
whenNotToUse: For a row use HStack, and for a row that wraps use MonarchFlowLayout (see inline). For many rows that scroll use LazyVStack in a ScrollView, or List.
api: VStack(alignment: HorizontalAlignment = .center, spacing: CGFloat? = nil, content: () -> Content)
appearance: A stack draws nothing. Its children look the same in every theme as they do outside it.
platformNotes: The web Stack has gap, align, justify, dividers and an element name. On iOS gap is the spacing argument with a value from theme.spacing, align is the alignment argument (leading, center, trailing), and justify is a Spacer or a frame with an alignment. dividers is a MonarchDivider written between the children. Stretching children to the full width is frame(maxWidth: .infinity) on each child. Android uses Column with Arrangement.spacedBy in the same way.
accessibility: A stack adds no accessibility element; children keep their own and are read from top to bottom.
Leading and trailing alignment follow the layout direction.
edgeCases: Without a spacing argument SwiftUI picks a default that differs between kinds of views; always pass one from the scale.
A VStack is as wide as its widest child. Add frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading) to fill the width.
VStack builds all its children at once; use LazyVStack for long scrolling content.
